fields.title: Rise Up, Men of God
fields.description: Rise Up, Men of God is a compelling biblical call to spiritual leadership for men everywhere. Drawing from Scripture, church history, and everyday life, this inspiring book equips men to lead their families, churches, and communities with faith, courage, humility, and purpose.

fields.title: Created to Lead
fields.body_html:
The Biblical Foundation of Male Spiritual Leadership

"The Lord God took the man and put him in the Garden of Eden to work it and take care of it. And the Lord God commanded the man, 'You are free to eat from any tree in the garden; but you must not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, for when you eat from it you will certainly die.'"

— Genesis 2:15–17 To understand what God asks of a man, we must go back to the beginning. Before polygamy was introduced by Lamech in Genesis 4, before the Fall, before sin entered the human story, God designed a world, and He designed a man to lead it.

Notice how the Bible tells the story. In Genesis 1, male and female are created together on the same day, both in the image of God, both given dominion over the earth. This is our foundation: a man and a woman are equal in dignity, equal in value, equal in their bearing of God's image. No husband should ever treat his wife as less than himself. No father should ever treat his daughters as less than his sons. In the image of God, we are the same.

But in Genesis 2, God gives us a closer look at how He arranged the first family, and here we see something important. God formed Adam first. He placed Adam in the garden. He gave the command about the tree to Adam, before Eve was even created. He gave Adam the work of naming the animals. Then He said, "It is not good for the man to be alone," and He made Eve from Adam's side — not from his head to rule over him, not from his feet to be trampled, but from his side to walk beside him.

From this order, the apostle Paul draws a conclusion in the New Testament. Writing to Timothy, he says, "For Adam was formed first, then Eve" (1 Timothy 2:13). Paul is teaching that God's design for male leadership in the home and church is rooted not in culture, not in sin, not in who is bigger or stronger, but in creation itself. Before the Fall, God had already given the man a particular responsibility.

And what was that responsibility? The text is clear. Adam was placed in the garden "to work it and take care of it" (Genesis 2:15). The Hebrew word for "take care of" (shamar) means to guard, to keep, to protect. Adam was to be a worker and a watchman. He was to cultivate and to protect.

This is still the calling of every man — to build up, and to guard.

Now watch carefully what happened in Genesis 3. The serpent came to Eve. She listened. She took the fruit. She ate. And then the Bible says something that many men have never noticed: "She also gave some to her husband, who was with her, and he ate it" (Genesis 3:6).

Who was with her? Adam. Where was he when his wife was being deceived by the serpent?

Standing right there. Doing what? Nothing. Saying nothing. Leading nothing. Protecting nothing.

He was silent when he should have spoken. He was passive when he should have acted. He was a coward when he should have been a man.

Brothers, this is the first sin of masculine leadership, and it is still our most common failure. Not that we are too aggressive, but that we are too passive. Not that we lead too much, but that we lead too little. Our wives are being deceived by the lies of this age, and we are standing next to them saying nothing. Our children are being discipled by social media, bad friends, and worse teachers, and we are sitting on the sofa scrolling our phones. Our churches are being weakened by compromise, and we are silent in the pew.

And then notice what Adam did when God confronted him. He blamed his wife. "The woman you put here with me — she gave me some fruit from the tree" (Genesis 3:12). He even blamed God.

A passive man becomes a blaming man. He will not take responsibility for his home, for his church, for his sin. He points his finger at his wife, at his boss, at the government, at the missionaries, at anyone but himself.

But observe this closely. When God came looking in the garden, whom did He call? "The Lord God called to the man, 'Where are you?'" (Genesis 3:9). God did not call Eve first, even though Eve sinned first. God called Adam. Why? Because Adam was the head. Adam was the one who had been given the command. Adam was responsible. In the same way, when judgment came on the human race, Paul tells us it came "through one man" — through Adam, not through Eve (Romans 5:12). The woman sinned first, but the man was held accountable.

This is sobering for us, brothers. God holds men accountable for what happens in their homes, their churches, their communities. We cannot escape it by blaming our wives. We cannot escape it by blaming our culture. We cannot escape it by blaming our fathers who did not teach us. The Lord is asking you, today, "Where are you?"

But thanks be to God, the story of Adam is not the last word. The Bible tells us of a second Adam — the Lord Jesus Christ. Where the first Adam failed, the last Adam succeeded (1 Corinthians 15:45). Where the first Adam was silent, Christ spoke truth. Where the first Adam hid, Christ stepped forward. Where the first Adam took from his bride and ruined her, Christ gave Himself for His Bride to save her. Where the first Adam brought death, Christ brought life.

Every man who trusts in Jesus is united to the second Adam. Your failure in leadership is not the end of your story. The grace of Christ covers your cowardice, and the Spirit of Christ gives you power to lead. You do not lead in your own strength. You lead in His.

So hear the call, brother. God created you to lead — not to dominate, not to oppress, not to boss your wife around, not to beat your children — but to cultivate and to guard. To build up your family spiritually. To watch over your home. To go to God first before the enemy comes to your wife. To take responsibility when things go wrong. To model Christ.

You were created for this. Will you rise up?

A Prayer

Father, I confess that I have been more like the first Adam than the second. I have been silent when I should have spoken. I have been passive when I should have led.

I have blamed others for what You have given me to carry. Forgive me, Lord. Wash me in the blood of Jesus, the second Adam, who succeeded where I failed. Fill me with Your Holy Spirit, that I may lead my home, my church, and my community as You have called me. Teach me to cultivate what You have entrusted to me. Teach me to guard it. And when You come looking for me, may I no longer be found hiding.

Here I am, Lord — send me. In the name of Jesus Christ, Amen.

fields.title: The Inner Man
fields.body_html:
Character Before Charisma

"The Lord does not look at the things people look at. People look at the outward appearance, but the Lord looks at the heart."

— 1 Samuel 16:7 When the prophet Samuel went to the house of Jesse to anoint a new king over Israel, he saw Eliab, the oldest son — tall, strong, handsome, the kind of man we would quickly call a leader. Samuel said to himself, "Surely the Lord's anointed stands here before the Lord." But God corrected him.

"Do not consider his appearance or his height, for I have rejected him. The Lord does not look at the things people look at. People look at the outward appearance, but the Lord looks at the heart" (1 Samuel 16:6–7).

Brother, this is where true spiritual leadership begins: not in your arms, not in your wallet, not in your title, not in your degree, not in your clan, but in your heart. God will not use a man whose heart is rotten, no matter how impressive he looks on the outside. And God will use a man whose heart is right, no matter how unimpressive he looks on the outside.

We live in an age that worships charisma. The loud preacher draws the crowd. The flashy businessman is envied. The man with the biggest car is respected. But God is not impressed with any of this. God is looking for character.

What is character? Character is who you are when no one is watching. Character is what you do when the lights are off, when you are alone in a hotel room in a different city, when your phone is in your hand and no one will ever know, when the money is on the table and the accountant has left the room. Character is the fruit of the Spirit — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control (Galatians 5:22–23) — grown slowly in the soil of your heart over years of walking with Jesus.

The apostle Paul, when he listed the qualifications for an elder in the church, said almost nothing about gifting and almost everything about character. Read 1 Timothy 3 slowly. An elder must be "above reproach, faithful to his wife, temperate, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach, not given to drunkenness, not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money" (1 Timothy 3:2–3). Notice: able to teach appears only once in this long list. The rest is character. If you cannot keep your temper at home, you are not qualified to lead anywhere else.

The same pattern appears in Titus 1, where Paul says an elder must be "blameless, faithful to his wife, a man whose children believe and are not open to the charge of being wild and disobedient" (Titus 1:6). God looks at how a man is doing as a husband and father before He considers him for leadership in the church. Your home is your first ministry. If your character is not being formed there, it is not being formed at all.

Consider the life of Archbishop Janani Luwum of Uganda. He was born in 1922 in Acholi, in the north of the country. He was converted as a young schoolteacher and was deeply shaped by the East African Revival. What made him great was not that he had a famous name or a powerful position — both of those came later. What made him great was that for decades before he ever stood before Idi Amin, he was walking with Jesus, confessing his sin, loving his wife Mary Florence, and raising his children in the fear of the Lord. By the time Amin tried to intimidate him in 1977, Luwum had the inner man of a lion. He said, "I can see the hand of God in this. Even if I die, I will not be afraid." When his moment came, he did not flinch, because his heart had been prepared long before in secret.

Charisma can carry you to the top. Only character can keep you there.

The apostle Peter understood this. In 2 Peter 1, he gives us a beautiful chain of virtues: "make every effort to add to your faith goodness; and to goodness, knowledge; and to knowledge, self-control; and to self-control, perseverance; and to perseverance, godliness; and to godliness, mutual affection; and to mutual affection, love" (2 Peter 1:5–7). Notice the verb: "make every effort."

Character does not happen by accident. It is cultivated, like a garden, by daily labor in prayer, in the Word, in confession, in obedience.

Augustine of Hippo, the great North African father of the Church, spent the first years of his adult life chasing sinful pleasures, ambition, and worldly wisdom. He had brilliance, but he lacked character. It was only when he met Christ in a garden in Milan, weeping and crying, "Take and read, take and read," and opening his Bible to Romans 13, that the Lord began to form in him the inner man that would later write the Confessions and The City of God and shape the Church for centuries. Augustine is a reminder to every man: your past does not disqualify you, but your character must be rebuilt from the inside out.

Let me ask you some hard questions, brother. When you are alone on your phone, what do you look at? When your wife disagrees with you, how do you respond? When a woman who is not your wife smiles at you, what do you do with your eyes? When the bribe is offered, what do you say? When your child disobeys, do you correct with patience or explode with rage? When the offering plate comes around, do you give, or do you grip? When someone insults you, do you return evil or bless?

These small moments, multiplied over years, are who you really are. These are the inner man. No title from men can replace it. No amount of noisy religion can disguise it. God sees it. Your wife sees it. Your children see it. And one day, the whole of heaven and earth will see it.

But here is the good news. You are not left alone to build your character. "God's divine power has given us everything we need for a godly life through our knowledge of him who called us by his own glory and goodness" (2 Peter 1:3). In Christ, you have everything you need. The Holy Spirit lives in you. The Word of God is given to you. The Church of God surrounds you. The means of grace are available to you. If your character is weak, it is not because God has withheld anything.

It is because you have not pressed into what He has already provided.

So do not be discouraged. Begin today. Begin with confession. Begin with the Word. Begin with prayer. Begin in the secret place. And let God slowly, patiently, build in you a man whose outside and inside match — a man whose wife trusts him, whose children honor him, whose church can rely on him, and whose Savior can say, "Well done, good and faithful servant."

A Prayer

Father, You see what no one else sees. You know what no one else knows. You have looked into my heart, and You have seen the truth about me. Where I am a hypocrite, expose me. Where I am proud, humble me. Where I am lazy in my soul, stir me up. Lord Jesus, You were tempted in every way as I am, yet You were without sin. Form Your character in me by the power of Your Holy Spirit. Make my outside and my inside the same. Make me a man of integrity — whole, undivided, true. Help me to build my inner man in the secret place, so that when my moment comes, I will not fall. In Your holy name I pray, amen.

fields.title: The Man Who Prays
fields.body_html:
Power on His Knees

"Therefore I want the men everywhere to pray, lifting up holy hands without anger or disputing."

— 1 Timothy 2:8 There is one practice that has defined every great man of God in the Bible and every great man of God in church history: he prayed. Not occasionally. Not desperately only in emergencies. Not merely in public to be heard. He prayed — deeply, daily, privately, persistently.

Abraham prayed. When God told him He was about to destroy Sodom, Abraham stood before the Lord and interceded for a city full of strangers (Genesis 18:22–33). Moses prayed. When Israel made the golden calf and God threatened to destroy them, Moses lay on his face for forty days and nights (Deuteronomy 9:18). David prayed. Read the Psalms — they are a man's prayer journal soaked in tears, praise, confession, and faith. Daniel prayed. Three times a day, with his window open toward Jerusalem, even when it cost him the lions' den (Daniel 6:10). Nehemiah prayed.

Before he spoke to the king, before he laid a single stone, he lifted his heart to God (Nehemiah 2:4).

And above them all, our Lord Jesus Christ prayed. The Son of God, perfect in every way, needing nothing, rose before dawn to pray (Mark 1:35), went up into the mountains alone to pray (Luke 6:12), prayed all night before choosing the twelve apostles, prayed for Peter, prayed for His disciples, prayed for you and me in John 17, and prayed in Gethsemane until His sweat became like drops of blood. If the Son of God needed to pray, how can we — weak, sinful, foolish — imagine we can lead without prayer?

A man who does not pray is not a spiritual leader, no matter what he calls himself. He may be a good provider, a strong disciplinarian, a respected businessman. But if he is not on his knees before God, he is leading his family into darkness while stumbling himself.

Paul's instruction to Timothy is striking. He says, "I want the men everywhere to pray, lifting up holy hands without anger or disputing" (1 Timothy 2:8). Paul singles out men. Not because women do not pray — they pray powerfully, and we know it — but because Paul is telling us that visible, leading, holy-handed prayer in the worship of the church is the duty of men. And if we will not pray publicly in the gathering of God's people, it is usually because we are not praying privately in our own closets.

Let me speak directly to husbands and fathers now. Your wife is praying for you. Your mother has been praying for you since before you were born. The women of your church are on their knees for the men. They are carrying the spiritual weight of the home while we discuss politics and football. This must change.

When was the last time you prayed with your wife? Not a quick prayer before food, but a real prayer — holding her hand, confessing your sins, praising God, interceding for your children, asking for His will to be done in your home? Peter warns husbands to treat their wives with understanding, "so that nothing will hinder your prayers" (1 Peter 3:7). Think about that. How you treat your wife can block your prayers from being heard. Many of our prayers have hit the ceiling because there was unrepented sin against the woman in our own bed.

When was the last time you laid hands on your children and prayed a blessing over them? Jacob blessed his sons before he died (Genesis 49). Jesus took children in His arms and blessed them (Mark 10:16). A father's blessing is a powerful thing in Scripture. Do not withhold it. Lay hands on your children at night, pray over them by name, speak God's favor over their lives. Many of our sons and daughters have gone astray because a father's blessing was missing.

The East African Revival, which touched Rwanda, Uganda, Kenya, Burundi, and Tanzania in the 1930s and 40s, was fundamentally a prayer movement. Simeon Nsibambi of Uganda and Dr. Joe Church, a missionary in Rwanda, would meet in a room in Kampala and pray for hours. Men gathered in small huts at dawn to cry out to God, to confess their sins, to walk in the light with one another. William Nagenda, who later became one of the greatest preachers of the revival, was a man marked by prayer. Festo Kivengere — who would later preach the gospel from Uganda to America and Europe — was a man of prayer. These were not professional clergymen at first. They were ordinary Ugandan men who decided that they would not lead their families or their nation without first falling on their knees. And from their prayers, a continent was shaken.

George Müller of Bristol, England, ran orphanages for thousands of children in the 1800s without ever asking anyone for money. When the cupboards were empty and breakfast was about to be served, he would gather the children and pray. Over and over, the food arrived — sometimes a baker knocking at the door saying, "God woke me in the night and told me the orphans needed bread," sometimes a milkman whose cart had broken down outside and who asked if they could use the milk before it spoiled. Müller kept records of over fifty thousand specific answers to prayer in his lifetime. He said, "The business of my life is to trust the Lord." Brother, if a man in England could trust God like that, can you not trust Him for your small shop, your farm, your job, your family — wherever God has placed you?

Let me give you a simple pattern for prayer as a husband and father. First, pray alone each morning.

Even fifteen minutes, before your phone comes on, before the radio goes on. Open your Bible, read a Psalm, turn it into prayer, confess your sins, praise God, lay out your day. fields.title: Loving Her as Christ Loved the Church
fields.body_html:
The Husband's Calling

"Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her to make her holy, cleansing her by the washing with water through the word."

— Ephesians 5:25–26 There is no higher standard for a husband in all the Bible than this: love your wife as Christ loved the Church. And there is no clearer demonstration of that love than a cross.

Paul gives us this command in Ephesians 5, in a passage that has become controversial in our day but is in fact one of the most beautiful pictures of marriage ever written. He says, "Wives, submit yourselves to your own husbands as you do to the Lord. For the husband is the head of the wife as Christ is the head of the church." Many men stop reading there and puff out their chests. "Did you hear that, woman? I am the head. You must submit." But Paul does not stop there, and neither should we. He keeps writing. "Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her."

Brother, look at the model Paul gives us. The head of the wife is like Christ, the head of the Church.

And how does Christ lead His Church? By giving Himself up for her. By taking her sin on His own body. By being crucified in her place. By washing her, not with power, but with sacrifice. By speaking the Word of God to her gently, patiently, daily. By preparing her as a radiant bride, without spot or wrinkle.

If this is the model, then "headship" has nothing to do with bossing your wife around. It has everything to do with laying down your life for her. The husband is the head not as a dictator but as a servant-leader. Not as a master but as a protector. Not as a man who takes but as a man who gives, gives, and gives again until he has nothing left.

Let us be honest about our cultures, brothers. In many places around the world, we have inherited practices that are not Christian, though they wear Christian clothes. The harshness some men show toward their wives, the physical violence that is still too common, the customs that treat a wife as a possession to be bought, the expectation that a wife is a servant to fetch water and bear children but not a partner to share life — these are not the gospel. They are not the way of Christ.

They are corruptions of a good creation, and they must be repented of.

The apostle Peter wrote, "Husbands, in the same way be considerate as you live with your wives, and treat them with respect as the weaker partner and as heirs with you of the gracious gift of life, so that nothing will hinder your prayers" (1 Peter 3:7). Three things shine here. First, live with her — not leaving her alone while you drink with friends, not away from home for months, but with her, sharing life. Second, be considerate — which in the Greek means "according to knowledge," meaning take time to know her heart, her fears, her joys, her body, her soul. Third, treat her with respect. She is an heir with you of eternal life. She will be a queen in the kingdom of heaven. Treat her now as you would treat a queen.

And do not forget that the ancient world Peter wrote to was harsher than ours. Wives could be divorced for burning dinner. Husbands ruled like kings. Into this Peter brings the gentleness of Christ. If the early Church could reform Roman marriage, the gospel can reform our marriages too.

I want you to notice one more thing in Ephesians 5. Paul says Christ cleanses the Church "by the washing with water through the word" (Ephesians 5:26). How does a husband participate in his wife's sanctification? By bringing the Word of God to her. This is why a husband must be a man of the Word. How will you wash your wife with Scripture if you do not know Scripture? How will you speak life over her in her discouragement if you cannot open the Bible? How will you remind her of the promises of God when she is fearful if the Bible is dusty on the shelf?

Martin Luther, the great German reformer, loved his wife Katharina deeply. He called her his "morning star," his "dear rib," and he relied on her as a true partner. Luther wrote, "There is no more lovely, friendly, and charming relationship, communion, or company than a good marriage."

He read Scripture with her. He prayed with her. He joked with her. He grieved with her when their daughter Magdalene died. Luther the theologian was also Luther the husband, and the same gospel he preached in the pulpit he lived in the kitchen. This is our call.

Let me speak even more practically. Husband, when was the last time you told your wife you love her? Not assumed it. Not showed it through providing money. Said it, looked her in the eye, with tenderness? When was the last time you apologized to her — not offered a defensive "sorry if you were offended" but a true confession, "I was wrong, please forgive me"? When was the last time you asked her about her fears, her hopes, her dreams, not about food or children or bills, but about her heart?

Your wife is not your housemaid. She is your sister in Christ before she is your wife. She is going to stand beside you in the resurrection. She is a fellow heir of the grace of life. Lead her toward Jesus, not toward exhaustion. Serve her as Christ served the Church.

I know some of you reading this are thinking, "But you do not know my wife. She is difficult. She does not respect me. She does not cook like my mother. She does not listen." Brother, Christ did not wait for the Church to be lovely before He loved her. "While we were still sinners, Christ died for us" (Romans 5:8). He loved us when we were His enemies. If He only loved those who deserved it, none of us would be saved. So also, you are called to love your wife not because she deserves it, but because Christ does. Your love for your wife is an act of worship to Jesus.

And to the young men who are not yet married, let me say this. Do not enter marriage lightly. Do not marry a woman because she is beautiful. Beauty fades. Do not marry a woman because she is rich. Riches fly. Do not marry a woman because your parents chose her for you without your consent. Marry a woman who fears the Lord (Proverbs 31:30), whose character you have observed over time, whom you can love as Christ loves the Church — for life. And before you take that vow, ask yourself: am I ready to die for her? Because that is what the vow means.

Finally, let me remind you of the promise. When a husband loves his wife as Christ loved the Church, something miraculous happens. The wife blooms. The home becomes peaceful. The children feel secure. The church is strengthened. The watching world sees a picture of the gospel.

Your marriage is a stage on which the love of Jesus is displayed. Do not ruin the play. Love her well.

A Prayer

Lord Jesus, You loved Your Bride the Church and gave Yourself up for her. You washed her, cleansed her, spoke tenderly to her, and are preparing her for glory.

Forgive me for the ways I have failed to love my wife like You. Where I have been harsh, soften my heart. Where I have been absent, bring me home. Where I have been silent, give me words of life. Where I have exploited my authority, teach me servant-leadership. Fill me with Your Spirit, that I may love my wife not as the world loves but as You love — sacrificially, patiently, tenderly, for her sanctification and Your glory. And make our marriage a living picture of the gospel in a dark and watching world. In Your name I pray, Amen.

fields.title: Raising Arrows
fields.body_html:
The Father's Sacred Duty

"Children are a heritage from the Lord, offspring a reward from him. Like arrows in the hands of a warrior are children born in one's youth. Blessed is the man whose quiver is full of them."

— Psalm 127:3–5 Of all the gifts God gives a man, few are greater than children. And of all the responsibilities God gives a man, none is weightier than fatherhood.

The psalmist compares children to arrows in the hand of a warrior. Think carefully about that picture. An arrow is not aimless. An arrow is sharpened, shaped, fitted, aimed, and released toward a target. A warrior who throws arrows blindly is no warrior at all. A father who brings children into the world but does not shape them, sharpen them, aim them at the glory of God is a warrior with a quiver he cannot use.

Yet how many of our homes today are full of unformed arrows? Fathers have brought children into the world and then abandoned their shaping to the mother, to the school, to the church, to the television, to the streets. So many nations are overrun with young men who have never been fathered.

They know how to survive, but they do not know how to live. They know how to take, but they do not know how to love. They have seen anger, but they have not seen tenderness. They have been beaten, but they have not been blessed. And they grow up to be like the men who made them.

This cycle must be broken, and God has put the axe in your hand.

The foundational passage on fatherhood in the Bible is Deuteronomy 6:4–9. Every Jewish father knew it by heart. Every Christian father should know it by heart too. "Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one. Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength. These commandments that I give you today are to be on your hearts. Impress them on your children. Talk about them when you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up. Tie them as symbols on your hands and bind them on your foreheads. Write them on the doorframes of your houses and on your gates."

Notice carefully, father. Before you can impress God's word on your children, it must be on your own heart. A man cannot give what he does not have. If the Bible is not shaping you, it will not shape your children through you. This is the first work of fatherhood — to be a man of the Word yourself.

Then notice the times: when you sit at home, when you walk along the road, when you lie down, when you get up. That is, all the time. Fatherhood is not a Sunday morning event. It is not outsourced to the pastor. It is the quiet, daily, thousand-times-repeated work of teaching your children who God is, why He made them, what He has said, and how they should live. In the evening around the fire. In the morning at the breakfast table. On the ride or the walk to school. In the garden as you dig together. Everywhere, always, you are discipling them.

Paul writes to the Ephesians, "Fathers, do not exasperate your children; instead, bring them up in the training and instruction of the Lord" (Ephesians 6:4). There are two sides to this. The negative side: do not exasperate. Do not provoke them to anger by your harshness, your unfairness, your absence, your favoritism, your drunkenness, your rage. Many fathers in every culture have exasperated their children through physical and verbal abuse, and it is one of the chief reasons young people walk away from the church. They associate God the Father with their earthly father, and if their earthly father was a terror, they run from God too. This must not be.

The positive side: bring them up in the training and instruction of the Lord. The word "training" means discipline, shaping, molding — it is an active, intentional forming of character. The word "instruction" means teaching, explanation, warning. A father must do both. He must teach them and he must shape them. And he must do it "of the Lord" — not according to his own preferences or his own frustrations, but according to what the Lord has commanded.

Discipline is part of love. "The Lord disciplines the one he loves, and he chastens everyone he accepts as his son" (Hebrews 12:6). A father who does not discipline his children does not love them. But discipline is not abuse. Biblical discipline is done in love, not in rage. It is done for the child's good, not for the father's relief. It is followed by restoration, not by lingering bitterness. It is always tied to teaching, so the child understands not just that he is being punished, but why his behavior is wrong.

In many cultures, the cane and the strap have been used freely for generations. I will not debate every cultural practice here, but I will say this: many fathers crossed a line from biblical discipline into cruelty, and their children have carried those scars into adulthood. Hear the Word of God: "Fathers, do not embitter your children, or they will become discouraged" (Colossians 3:21). If your child is afraid of you more than they love you, something is wrong.

Let me give you some practical aims for your children. Aim them at Christ. The first goal of fatherhood is their salvation. Pray it over them every day. Teach them the gospel over and over.

Do not assume they are Christians just because they were born into a Christian home. Lead each child to personal faith in Jesus.

Aim them with wisdom. Proverbs was written by a father, Solomon, for his son. Read Proverbs together. Teach them about the choice between the way of the wise and the way of the fool, between diligence and laziness, between purity and adultery, between the fear of the Lord and the folly of the scoffer.

Aim them at usefulness. Teach them to work with their hands. Teach them to serve others. Teach them to manage money. Teach them to be humble. Teach your sons how to treat women — in how you treat their mother. Teach your daughters what a godly man looks like — in who you are. Your life is the curriculum. Your words are secondary.

Aim them at the local church. Do not let them see Christianity as a family-only affair. Take them to church every week. Introduce them to godly mentors. Let them see you serving, giving, worshipping, submitting to other leaders. If they see that church is important to you, it will be important to them.

Brother, consider the father in the parable of the prodigal son (Luke 15). When his younger son returned in shame and rags, the father ran to him, embraced him, kissed him, restored him. That is the heart of God. And that is the heart a father must have. Sometimes our children will disappoint us. Sometimes they will break our hearts. The call of a father is not to write them off, but to watch the road with eyes full of hope, ready to run when they turn home.

Your children did not ask to be born. God gave them to you, and He will ask you one day what you did with them. Not what you bought for them, but what you built into them. Not how many you had, but what they became. Be a father worth having. Aim your arrows well. And one day, by God's grace, your quiver will be full of arrows flying for the glory of God.

A Prayer

Heavenly Father, You are the Father from whom every family in heaven and on earth takes its name. You have given me children as a heritage and a responsibility.

Forgive me for every time I have been too busy, too harsh, too distant, too angry, too silent. Forgive me for exasperating them instead of shepherding them. Give me the grace to disciple them — to read Your Word with them, to pray with them, to correct them with love, to model Christ before them. Save my children, Lord. May not one of them be lost. Use me as Your instrument to shape them into arrows that will fly far and hit the target of Your glory. In the name of Jesus Christ, our elder Brother, Amen.

So many nations are overrun with young men who have never been fathered. They know how to survive, but they do not know how to live. They know how to take, but they do not know how to love. They have seen anger, but they have not seen tenderness. They have been beaten, but they have not been blessed. And they grow up to be like the men who made them. This cycle must be broken, and God has put the axe in your hand. The foundational passage on fatherhood in the Bible is Deuteronomy 6:4–9. Every Jewish father knew it by heart. Every Christian father should know it by heart too. "Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one. Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength. These commandments that I give you today are to be on your hearts. Impress them on your children. Talk about them when you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up. Tie them as symbols on your hands and bind them on your foreheads. Write them on the doorframes of your houses and on your gates." Notice carefully, father. Before you can impress God's word on your children, it must be on your own heart. A man cannot give what he does not have. If the Bible is not shaping you, it will not shape your children through you. This is the first work of fatherhood — to be a man of the Word yourself. Then notice the times: when you sit at home, when you walk along the road, when you lie down, when you get up. That is, all the time. Fatherhood is not a Sunday morning event. It is not outsourced to the pastor. It is the quiet, daily, thousand-times-repeated work of teaching your children who God is, why He made them, what He has said, and how they should live. In the evening around the fire. In the morning at the breakfast table. On the ride or the walk to school. In the garden as you dig together. Everywhere, always, you are discipling them. Paul writes to the Ephesians, "Fathers, do not exasperate your children; instead, bring them up in the training and instruction of the Lord" (Ephesians 6:4). There are two sides to this. The negative side: do not exasperate. Do not provoke them to anger by your harshness, your unfairness, your absence, your favoritism, your drunkenness, your rage. Many fathers in every culture have exasperated their children through physical and verbal abuse, and it is one of the chief reasons young people walk away from the church. They associate God the Father with their earthly father, and if their earthly father was a terror, they run from God too. This must not be. The positive side: bring them up in the training and instruction of the Lord. The word "training" means discipline, shaping, molding — it is an active, intentional forming of character. The word "instruction" means teaching, explanation, warning. A father must do both. He must teach them and he must shape them. And he must do it "of the Lord" — not according to his own preferences or his own frustrations, but according to what the Lord has commanded. Discipline is part of love. "The Lord disciplines the one he loves, and he chastens everyone he accepts as his son" (Hebrews 12:6). A father who does not discipline his children does not love them. But discipline is not abuse. Biblical discipline is done in love, not in rage. It is done for the child's good, not for the father's relief. It is followed by restoration, not by lingering bitterness. It is always tied to teaching, so the child understands not just that he is being punished, but why his behavior is wrong. In many cultures, the cane and the strap have been used freely for generations. I will not debate every cultural practice here, but I will say this: many fathers crossed a line from biblical discipline into cruelty, and their children have carried those scars into adulthood. Hear the Word of God: "Fathers, do not embitter your children, or they will become discouraged" (Colossians 3:21). If your child is afraid of you more than they love you, something is wrong. Do not assume they are Christians just because they were born into a Christian home. Lead each child to personal faith in Jesus. Aim them with wisdom. Proverbs was written by a father, Solomon, for his son. Read Proverbs together. Teach them about the choice between the way of the wise and the way of the fool, between diligence and laziness, between purity and adultery, between the fear of the Lord and the folly of the scoffer. Aim them at usefulness. Teach them to work with their hands. Teach them to serve others. Teach them to manage money. Teach them to be humble. Teach your sons how to treat women — in how you treat their mother. Teach your daughters what a godly man looks like — in who you are. Your life is the curriculum. Your words are secondary. Aim them at the local church. Do not let them see Christianity as a family-only affair. Take them to church every week. Introduce them to godly mentors. Let them see you serving, giving, worshipping, submitting to other leaders. If they see that church is important to you, it will be important to them. Brother, consider the father in the parable of the prodigal son (Luke 15). When his younger son returned in shame and rags, the father ran to him, embraced him, kissed him, restored him. That is the heart of God. And that is the heart a father must have. Sometimes our children will disappoint us. Sometimes they will break our hearts. The call of a father is not to write them off, but to watch the road with eyes full of hope, ready to run when they turn home. Your children did not ask to be born. God gave them to you, and He will ask you one day what you did with them. Not what you bought for them, but what you built into them. Not how many you had, but what they became. Be a father worth having. Aim your arrows well. And one day, by God's grace, your quiver will be full of arrows flying for the glory of God. A Prayer Heavenly Father, You are the Father from whom every family in heaven and on earth takes its name. You have given me children as a heritage and a responsibility. Forgive me for every time I have been too busy, too harsh, too distant, too angry, too silent. Forgive me for exasperating them instead of shepherding them. Give me the grace to disciple them — to read Your Word with them, to pray with them, to correct them with love, to model Christ before them. Save my children, Lord. May not one of them be lost. Use me as Your instrument to shape them into arrows that will fly far and hit the target of Your glory. In the name of Jesus Christ, our elder Brother, Amen.

fields.title: Strength Under Control
fields.body_html:
Gentleness as a Mark of True Manhood

"Come to me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls."

— Matthew 11:28–29 What kind of man is Jesus? The King of kings. The Lord of lords. The Lion of Judah. The One who spoke galaxies into being. The One before whom every knee will bow. And how does He describe Himself? "I am gentle and humble in heart."

This is astonishing, brother. The strongest being in the universe calls Himself gentle. The One with all authority in heaven and on earth calls Himself humble. If Jesus is the perfect Man — and He is — then the perfect man is gentle. Not weak. Not soft. Not a coward. But strong in such a way that he does not need to prove it by crushing others.

We have a serious problem in many cultures. Many men confuse manhood with harshness. They think that to be respected, they must shout. To be obeyed, they must threaten. To be feared, they must hit. They raise their voices at their wives, backhand their children, bark at their workers, and call it "being a man." But this is not manhood. This is brokenness. It is a man out of control trying to pretend he is in control.

Look again at Jesus. He cleared the temple with a whip (John 2:15). He rebuked demons and silenced storms. He stared down Herod and called him "that fox" (Luke 13:32). He was not soft.

And yet the same Jesus took little children in His arms and blessed them. The same Jesus wept at the tomb of Lazarus. The same Jesus knelt and washed His disciples' feet, including the feet of Judas who would betray Him. The same Jesus said from the cross, "Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing" (Luke 23:34). Strength and gentleness were not enemies in Him.

They were friends.

Paul calls gentleness a fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23). You cannot produce it yourself. You can try to fake it for a while, but it will break under pressure. True gentleness is grown in a man only by the Holy Spirit working in him over time. The more a man walks with Jesus, the gentler he becomes. The more he sees his own sin and the depth of grace he has received, the less harsh he is with others. A proud man is always harsh. A humble man is almost always gentle.

Moses is called "a very humble man, more humble than anyone else on the face of the earth" (Numbers 12:3). This is the same Moses who led millions out of Egypt, who confronted Pharaoh, who smashed the tablets, who judged Israel. He was no weakling. But he was humble. He led from his knees more than from his shoulders. And God entrusted him with everything.

I want to speak honestly about something that grieves the heart of God in many of our homes: domestic violence. Brother, if you have ever hit your wife, listen to me. That is not manhood. That is not biblical headship. That is sin. The hand that God gave you to bless her, to work for her, to protect her, you have used to wound her. The body that Christ has given as His own temple, you have bruised. This is not a small matter. It is a sin against your wife, against God, and against the picture of Christ and His Church that your marriage is supposed to display.

There is grace for you. But grace comes with repentance. You must confess it — to God, to her, to your pastor, to a trusted brother in the church. You must submit to counsel and accountability.

If you are in a pattern of violence, you must get help now. Not tomorrow. Now. "An angry person stirs up conflict, and a hot-tempered person commits many sins" (Proverbs 29:22). God will not hold back His judgment from a man who harms the one he vowed to protect.

And fathers, hear me: the same applies to how you treat your children. The cane has its place within biblical, measured correction, but many of our fathers have crossed far over that line.

Children who grow up afraid of their father's hand often struggle for years to know a gentle God.

They imagine that God the Father is like Papa — unpredictable, angry, a terror. What a lie we have told them by our rage. Let us undo it by our gentleness from this day forward.

Think of Festo Kivengere, the great Ugandan evangelist. During the reign of terror under Idi Amin, after Archbishop Janani Luwum was murdered, Kivengere fled to Kenya for his life. He later wrote a book with a startling title: "I Love Idi Amin." Imagine that. A Ugandan bishop, whose friend was murdered by the dictator, saying publicly that he loved him. This was not a weakness. It was the strength of the gospel. Kivengere wrote, "On the cross, Jesus said, 'Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.' As evil as Amin was, I knew that I must love him." That is gentleness rooted in resurrection power. That is manhood under the lordship of Jesus.

Let me give you the marks of a gentle man.

A gentle man listens more than he speaks. He does not shout down his wife in an argument. He does not interrupt his children to have the last word. He listens carefully. He considers. He speaks truth, but he speaks it in love (Ephesians 4:15).

A gentle man keeps his word. His yes is yes and his no is no (Matthew 5:37). He does not need to swear, because he does not need to be loud to be believed.

A gentle man controls his temper. "Whoever is slow to anger is better than the mighty, and he who rules his spirit than he who takes a city" (Proverbs 16:32). A man who can conquer a city but not his own temper has conquered nothing. A man who can rule his own spirit is a true king.

A gentle man forgives. He does not hold grudges. He does not wait to avenge every insult. He remembers how much he has been forgiven by Christ, and it softens him toward others.

A gentle man is approachable. His wife is not afraid to tell him something has gone wrong. His children run to him, not away from him. His employees can speak the truth to him without fear.

His friends can rebuke him in love.

A gentle man prays under pressure. When the storm comes, he does not explode. He goes to his knees. The first response of a gentle man to trouble is prayer, not panic, not rage.

Brother, our world is full of hard men. We do not need any more of them. We need gentle men — men like Christ. Men whose strength is under His control. Men whose wives are honored, whose children are treasured, whose employees are respected, whose enemies are loved. Such men change a village. Such men change a nation.

A Prayer

Lord Jesus, You are gentle and humble in heart. You are strong beyond measure, and yet You never crushed a bruised reed or snuffed out a smoldering wick. Forgive me for the harshness in my words, the rage in my eyes, the cruelty in my hands.

Tame my temper, Lord. Break my pride. Teach me the true strength of gentleness.

Make me a man in whose presence my wife feels safe, my children feel loved, my enemies feel respected. Let Your Spirit bear the fruit of gentleness in me, that those who meet me may see something of You. In Your gentle and mighty name, amen.

fields.title: By the Sweat of Your Brow
fields.body_html:
Working Hard and Providing Well

"Anyone who does not provide for their relatives, and especially for their own household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever."

— 1 Timothy 5:8 These are sobering words. The apostle Paul does not say a man who fails to provide is a weak Christian, or a struggling Christian, or a Christian who needs encouragement. He says such a man has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.

Why such strong language? Because provision is one of the most basic callings of a man. Long before a man leads spiritually, he must provide materially. Long before he teaches the Bible to his family, he must put food on their table. These are not competing duties — they go together. A man who preaches a great sermon on Sunday but whose children go to bed hungry on Monday has failed. God has called him to both.

Work is not a curse. This is important for us to understand, because many men think of work as punishment, something to escape through winning the lottery, finding a rich marriage, or receiving remittances from a relative abroad. But in Genesis 2, before Adam sinned, God placed him in the garden "to work it and take care of it" (Genesis 2:15). Work came before the Fall. Work is part of how God made us. Work is dignifying. Work is worship.

What the Fall did was make work harder. God said to Adam, "By the sweat of your brow you will eat your food" (Genesis 3:19). The soil now produces thorns. The business now faces corruption.

The field now suffers drought. The office now has conflict. But work itself remains a gift. When we labor with our hands and our minds, we are imaging our Creator, who labored for six days and rested on the seventh.

The book of Proverbs has stern warnings about the lazy man. "Go to the ant, you sluggard; consider its ways and be wise! It has no commander, no overseer or ruler, yet it stores its provisions in summer and gathers its food at harvest" (Proverbs 6:6–8). "A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest — and poverty will come on you like a thief and scarcity like an armed man" (Proverbs 6:10–11). "The sluggard does not plow in season; so at harvest time he looks but finds nothing" (Proverbs 20:4).

Brother, in our day, we must confront a spirit of idleness that sits on many young men. They gather at the trading center and complain that there are no jobs. Some of them have phones in their hands and half a day to burn. They wait for handouts. They dream of going abroad to some richer country, but they will not dig the garden at home. They complain that life is unfair while the fields around their house lie untended. The Bible's answer to this is simple and strong: work.

Paul said to the Thessalonian church, "For even when we were with you, we gave you this rule: 'The one who is unwilling to work shall not eat.' We hear that some among you are idle and disruptive. They are not busy; they are busybodies. Such people we command and urge in the Lord Jesus Christ to settle down and earn the food they eat" (2 Thessalonians 3:10–12).

This is not harshness against the poor. The Bible commands us to care for the widow, the orphan, the disabled, the elderly, those truly unable to work. That is true religion (James 1:27). But for the able-bodied man who refuses to work, there is no Christian welfare. Get up. Plant. Trade. Learn a skill. Drive a taxi. Start small. Be faithful. God blesses faithful hands.

And when God does give you work, do it with all your heart. "Whatever you do, work at it with all your heart, as working for the Lord, not for human masters" (Colossians 3:23). Do not be the kind of worker who only works when the boss is looking. Do not steal time, steal materials, steal credit. Do not take bribes. Do not cheat customers. Your work is your testimony to the world.

Many people will never hear a sermon, but they will meet you at the market, at the office, at the shop. Is your work a signboard for Christ?

Let me speak also to men who have money. You are not exempt from this chapter. A rich man can be just as lazy as a poor man — sometimes more so. Solomon said, "A sated man loathes honey, but to a hungry man every bitter thing is sweet" (Proverbs 27:7). Wealth tests a man's soul. If God has given you success, you must still work. Your work may be different — leading a company, discipling younger men, serving on church boards, giving generously — but it must be real work, not self-indulgence.

Consider George Müller of Bristol, who I mentioned earlier. He trusted God for daily provision for thousands of orphans, yet he worked incredibly hard. His prayers did not replace labor. His prayers fueled labor. He was up at dawn, he handled correspondence, he managed staff, he preached, he wrote, he traveled thousands of miles. Prayer and work are not opposites in the Christian life. They are partners.

Consider also the apostle Paul. Though he was an apostle and had the right to be supported by the churches, he worked with his own hands as a tentmaker (Acts 18:3, 1 Thessalonians 2:9). He did not want to be a burden. He wanted to model the dignity of labor. He said to the Ephesian elders, "You yourselves know that these hands of mine have supplied my own needs and the needs of my companions" (Acts 20:34).

Now let us think about provision in the wider family. A Christian man in many cultures often has more than just his immediate family to consider. There is the wider family — aging parents, younger siblings in school, cousins with needs. This can become a heavy burden, but it is also a beautiful calling. Paul said, "Anyone who does not provide for their relatives, and especially for their own household." Relatives first, then household first among them. Your nuclear family must come before the wider family in your budget — otherwise you are robbing your wife and children to please your relatives. But you are not free to ignore those relatives either. Balance, wisdom, generosity, and limits all together.

Set goals. Work with a plan. "The plans of the diligent lead to profit as surely as haste leads to poverty" (Proverbs 21:5). Have a budget. Know what comes in and what goes out. Save something, even a little. "In the house of the wise are stores of choice food and oil, but a foolish man devours all he has" (Proverbs 21:20). Avoid debt where possible. Plan for your children's school fees. Plan for old age. Plan to give generously to God's work.

Give the first portion to God. The principle of the tithe runs through the Old Testament and is honored throughout the New. Honor the Lord with the first and best of what you earn (Proverbs 3:9). A man who will not tithe to his local church cannot claim to trust God with his money. It is a simple test of the heart.

Finally, do not love money. "The love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. Some people, eager for money, have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many griefs" (1 Timothy 6:10). You can work hard without worshiping money. You can pursue excellence without being ruled by greed. You provide so your family is fed and God is honored — not so you can boast against your neighbor. Many Christian men in our day have been destroyed by the prosperity gospel, a false teaching that turns Jesus into a business deal. Flee that false gospel. Work hard.

Trust God. Be content. Give generously. And let your life be a rebuke to both the sluggard and the greedy.

Brother, put your hand to the plow and do not look back. Your family is watching. Your neighbors are watching. Your Lord is watching. Work as unto Him, and He will bless the work of your hands.

A Prayer

Lord God, You who labored for six days and rested on the seventh, teach me the dignity of work. Break the spirit of laziness in me. Break the spirit of greed in me.

Give me strength for my hands, wisdom for my mind, integrity for my dealings. Let me work not for bread alone but as an act of worship to You. Provide for my household, O God. Let my wife and children never lack what they need. Use my hands to serve my family, my church, and the poor. Make me generous where I have been grasping. Make me diligent where I have been idle. And may the sweat of my brow be a sweet offering to You. In Jesus' name, Amen.

And may the sweat of my brow be a sweet offering to You. In Jesus' name, Amen.

fields.title: The Watchman at the Gate
fields.body_html:
Protecting Your Home

"After I looked things over, I stood up and said to the nobles, the officials and the rest of the people, 'Don't be afraid of them. Remember the Lord, who is great and awesome, and fight for your families, your sons and your daughters, your wives and your homes.'"

— Nehemiah 4:14 When Nehemiah led the returning exiles to rebuild the walls of Jerusalem, enemies surrounded them. Sanballat and Tobiah mocked them, then plotted to attack them. Nehemiah's response is a masterclass in godly manhood. He armed the men. He set watchmen on the walls. He stationed fighters at every gap. And he called out the charge: "Fight for your families, your sons and your daughters, your wives and your homes."

Brother, God has made you a watchman at the gate of your home. There are enemies — you cannot pretend otherwise. There is the enemy of the flesh, within us. There is the enemy of the world, around us. There is the enemy of the devil, against us. You stand on the wall, and your household stands behind you. You must watch, and you must fight.

Protection is one of the most basic callings of a man. It goes back to Adam, who was placed in the garden to "work it and take care of it" (Genesis 2:15). The word "take care of" in Hebrew is the same word used for watchmen, for those who guard. Adam was to protect the garden, and especially, he was to protect Eve from the serpent. He failed. We have often failed too. But God still calls us to this work, and He gives us grace to do it.

There are three levels of protection a man must provide for his household: physical, emotional, and spiritual. Let us look at each.

First, physical protection. You are the first line of defense for your wife and children against any physical threat — whether an intruder in the night, a dangerous road, a toxic environment, a health crisis. A man does not hide behind his wife when danger comes. He steps in front. A man does not send his children into harm while he sits safe. He leads them through.

Many of us do this instinctively when danger is obvious. But there are subtler physical threats we must guard against too. Does your family have clean water? Is your home secure? Do your children walk safe routes to school? Is your wife exhausted because she carries burdens you could share?

Physical protection is not only about chasing thieves. It is about building a safe, healthy, livable home.

Second, emotional protection. This is where many of us fail most seriously, often without realizing it. Your home should be the safest place in the world for your wife and children — not only safe from outside enemies, but safe from you. If your temper rages inside your own home, you have not protected your family. You have become the very thing they need protection from.

A man who protects his family emotionally watches what comes out of his mouth. "The tongue has the power of life and death" (Proverbs 18:21). Your words can build up your wife or tear her down. Your words can bless your children or curse them. Many of us carry wounds to this day from words a father spoke decades ago. Guard your tongue. Speak life.

A man who protects his family emotionally watches who comes into the home. Not every guest is a blessing. Not every relative is safe around your daughters. Not every friend is a good influence on your sons. You are the gatekeeper. If someone brings a spirit of drunkenness, lust, violence, or mockery into your house, it is your duty to keep them out. Do not be afraid to offend people when the safety of your family is at stake.

A man who protects his family emotionally listens when they speak of fear or pain. Do not dismiss your wife's concerns as "women's talk." Do not laugh when your son tells you what frightened him. Take them seriously. Their hearts are in your hands.

Third, spiritual protection. This is the deepest and most important. The apostle Paul writes, "Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the powers of this dark world and against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly realms" (Ephesians 6:12). There is a real devil. There are real demons. There are real spiritual attacks on your wife, your children, your home. And you are called to stand as a watchman on that wall.

How do you protect your family spiritually? First, by covering them in prayer. The devil does not fear your theology; he fears your prayers. Pray over every room of your home. Pray at the door as your children leave for school. Pray by their beds at night. Pray with your wife before you fall asleep. Prayer is the invisible armor over your family.

Second, by guarding what enters the home through media. The television, the internet, the smartphone — these are open doors, and the devil walks through them freely if no watchman is at the gate. Fathers, you must decide what your children watch, what apps they have, what songs they listen to. This is not oppression. This is love. "I will not look with approval on anything that is vile," said David (Psalm 101:3). Your home should be the same. You will answer to God for what you allowed to enter.

Third, by guarding the teaching your family receives. In our day, there is no shortage of false teachers. Prosperity preachers sell salvation. Self-appointed prophets claim private revelations.

Cults dress up like churches. You must be a Berean (Acts 17:11), testing everything by Scripture, and you must help your family do the same. Do not let your children be discipled by whatever loud voice shouts the latest on social media. Disciple them yourself. Take them to a faithful, Bible-preaching local church. Read solid Christian books with them. Answer their questions carefully.

Consider the Maccabees, the Jewish warriors of the intertestamental period, who defended their faith against the Greek king Antiochus Epiphanes. When Antiochus tried to force them to worship idols and abandon the Scriptures, one family — Mattathias and his sons — stood up. They said, "Let everyone who is zealous for the law and who stands by the covenant follow me!" (1 Maccabees 2:27). Mattathias, a father, risked everything for the spiritual protection of his household and his nation. His son Judas "Maccabeus" became famous for defending the people of God. Though they lived before Christ, their zeal for the Lord is a picture of what a watchman father looks like.

Consider the early Ugandan martyrs. When Kabaka Mwanga demanded that the young Christian pages renounce their faith and submit to his perverse demands, Mukasa, Lwanga, and the others refused, even knowing it would cost them their lives. Their refusal was not only for themselves — it was for the faith of a whole generation. They protected the gospel by their blood. Their watch cost them everything, and because of it, the Church in Uganda stands today.

Brother, you may never face martyrdom. But you will face daily skirmishes. A coworker invites you to a corrupt deal — the enemy is at the gate. A sensual advertisement pops up on your phone — the enemy is at the gate. A teacher tells your child that the Bible is a fairy tale — the enemy is at the gate. A friend mocks your faith — the enemy is at the gate. At each of these gates, a watchman is needed. That watchman is you.

Do not sleep on the wall. Do not wander off to your own pleasures and leave the walls unmanned.

Do not trade the safety of your home for the pleasures of the flesh. Stand firm. Pray. Fight the good fight of faith. And when you are weary, remember the words of Nehemiah to tired men: "Our God will fight for us" (Nehemiah 4:20).

A Prayer

Mighty God, You are a wall of fire around Your people. Teach me to be a watchman at the gate of my home. Make me alert to the schemes of the devil. Make me brave against the threats of this age. Make me quick to pray over my wife, my children, and every corner of my house. Where I have let evil through the gates, forgive me.

Where I have slept on the wall, awaken me. Where I have become the danger my family needed protection from, convict me and change me. Let my home be a fortress of Your peace, and let Your angels encamp around us. In the name of Jesus Christ, the Lord of hosts, amen.

fields.title: Accountability
fields.body_html:
No Man Stands Alone

"As iron sharpens iron, so one person sharpens another."

— Proverbs 27:17 One of the great lies a man can believe is that he does not need other men. He thinks he is strong enough, wise enough, holy enough to walk the Christian life alone. He will come to church on Sunday, but he will not open his life to anyone in particular during the week. He has no one who knows his struggles. He has no one who can correct him. He has no one who can pray specifically over his secret battles. He is an island, and he is sinking.

Brother, the devil loves a lone man. He picks off the stragglers. He destroys the isolated. He whispers to the private man that no one understands him, no one would forgive him, no one can help him. And slowly, steadily, the lone man is eaten by sins he never meant to let grow.

The Bible is clear that God has made us for community, and especially that men need other men.

"As iron sharpens iron, so one person sharpens another" (Proverbs 27:17). Iron does not sharpen itself. A knife left alone grows dull. A man left alone grows dull — in his love for Christ, in his holiness, in his zeal, in his courage. He needs the scraping, the grinding, the honest friction of another iron man.

David had Jonathan. "In everything Jonathan did, he had great success, because the Lord was with him" (1 Samuel 18:14), and the bond of their souls was such that "Jonathan became one in spirit with David, and he loved him as himself" (1 Samuel 18:1).

When David was hunted by Saul in the wilderness, Jonathan came to him and "helped him find strength in God" (1 Samuel 23:16). Every man needs a Jonathan — a brother who helps him find strength in God when life has crushed him.

Paul had Timothy and Titus and Silas and Barnabas and Luke. He was an apostle, a man of tremendous spiritual power, and yet he did not travel alone. He wrote his deepest affections to these men. Read 2 Timothy — it is a dying man's letter to his son in the faith, full of love and honesty. Paul, in his last days, said, "Only Luke is with me" (2 Timothy 4:11), and he asked Timothy to come quickly. Even the great apostle needed companions.

Jesus Himself, though He was the Son of God, gathered the Twelve and was especially close to Peter, James, and John. He did not lead alone. He did not die alone. He lived His earthly ministry surrounded by brothers.

If Jesus, David, and Paul all needed brothers, who are you to think you can live alone?

The most essential element of accountability is honesty. Until a man is willing to be honest with at least one other brother, he cannot grow. James writes, "Therefore confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed. The prayer of a righteous person is powerful and effective" (James 5:16). There is healing in confession. Not to a priest in a dark box, but to a brother in the light of day. When you say out loud to another Christian man, "I have been struggling with lust," or "I have been drinking in secret," or "I have been cheating on my taxes," or "I have been harsh with my wife and I do not know how to stop," something powerful happens. The sin's hiding place is exposed. The darkness flees. The healing begins.

The East African Revival was marked precisely by this kind of honesty. When the Spirit fell on Rwanda and Uganda in the 1930s, men began to confess their sins publicly. Some had stolen from their employers; they went to pay back what they had taken. Some had slept with women not their wives; they went to ask forgiveness. Some had grudges with fellow believers; they went to reconcile. They called it "walking in the light," based on 1 John 1:7: "If we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus, his Son, purifies us from all sin." And revival spread like fire. This kind of honesty is the fuel of revival, and without it, our churches will stay weak no matter how many programs we run.

So, brother, find at least two or three men in your local church and bind yourself to them. Do not pick only your closest personal friends — pick men you respect spiritually, men who will tell you the truth even when it hurts. Meet with them regularly. Some meet weekly, some monthly, some every other week. Whatever schedule fits, commit to it and keep it. Do not cancel the meeting because you are "too busy." You are never too busy to save your soul.

When you meet, go beyond small talk. Ask each other hard questions. The Methodist bands, started by John Wesley in the 1700s, used a set of probing questions that still convict today. They asked each other things like: "What known sins have you committed since our last meeting? What temptations have you met with? How were you delivered? What have you thought, said, or done, of which you doubt whether it be sin or not?" Wesley's movement transformed England partly because men were not allowed to hide.

And brothers, some of you need to ask forgiveness from other men. You have offended a brother in the church and have been avoiding him for years. This is not Christianity. Jesus said, "If you are offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother or sister has something against you, leave your gift there in front of the altar. First go and be reconciled to them; then come and offer your gift" (Matthew 5:23–24). If something stands between you and another believer, it also stands between you and God. Go to him. Humble yourself. Make it right. The relief on the other side is worth it.

Accountability is also about receiving correction. Proverbs says, "Whoever heeds discipline shows the way to life, but whoever ignores correction leads others astray" (Proverbs 10:17). "Do not rebuke mockers or they will hate you; rebuke the wise and they will love you" (Proverbs 9:8). Can a brother correct you? If you become angry and defensive every time someone points out a fault, you are a fool, not a leader. The wise man welcomes correction, even when it stings. He says, "Thank you for loving me enough to tell me. Let me pray about this. Let me repent of this."

Husbands, listen here too. Your wife is often your best accountability partner. She sees what no one else sees. She can tell when your prayer life is weak. She can tell when your heart is hard.

Receive her observations with grace. Do not be the husband who demands submission but refuses correction. A humble husband invites his wife's insight into his soul.

Finally, submit yourself to the authority of your local church. Not just attendance, but membership.

Place yourself under the shepherding of biblical elders. Be willing to be disciplined if you fall into serious sin. The book of Hebrews says, "Have confidence in your leaders and submit to their authority, because they keep watch over you as those who must give an account" (Hebrews 13:17).

A man who will not submit to any spiritual authority on earth is a law unto himself — and such a man is dangerous to his family and to the church.

No man stands alone. Not David. Not Paul. Not Jesus. Not Kivengere. Not Luwum. Not you. Find your brothers. Let them see you. Let them sharpen you. And together you will stand when alone you would fall.

A Prayer

Father, I confess that I have tried to walk this road alone. I have kept my sins hidden in the dark where they have grown in power. I have avoided honest friendships because I feared exposure. I have rejected correction because I loved my pride.

Forgive me, Lord. Give me at least one brother, and if possible many, with whom I can walk in the light. Make me honest. Make me teachable. Make me quick to confess and quick to forgive. Use iron in my life, even when it grinds, to make me sharp for Your service. And knit me deeply into the body of Christ, so that I may stand and not fall. In the name of Jesus, amen.
