fields.title: Men in the Church
fields.body_html:
Eldership and Service

"To the elders among you, I appeal as a fellow elder and a witness of Christ's sufferings who also will share in the glory to be revealed: Be shepherds of God's flock that is under your care, watching over them — not because you must, but because you are willing, as God wants you to be; not pursuing dishonest gain, but eager to serve."

— 1 Peter 5:1–2 God has ordered His Church with shepherds. From the earliest days, the apostles appointed elders in every city (Acts 14:23, Titus 1:5). These men — mature, proven, biblically qualified — are given the task of shepherding God's people. Not to be kings, but servants. Not to enrich themselves, but to feed the flock. Not to dominate, but to lead by example.

Brother, spiritual leadership in the home and spiritual leadership in the church are not two separate lives. They flow from the same well. The man who shepherds his wife and children well is the kind of man God chooses to shepherd His Church. And the man who serves faithfully in his local church is strengthened to serve better at home. The home prepares the man for the church; the church equips the man for the home.

Let us look carefully at who can be an elder in the Church of Christ. Paul writes to Timothy: "Here is a trustworthy saying: Whoever aspires to be an overseer desires a noble task. Now the overseer is to be above reproach, faithful to his wife, temperate, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach, not given to drunkenness, not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money. He must manage his own family well and see that his children obey him, and he must do so in a manner worthy of full respect. (If anyone does not know how to manage his own family, how can he take care of God's church?) He must not be a recent convert, or he may become conceited and fall under the same judgment as the devil. He must also have a good reputation with outsiders, so that he will not fall into disgrace and into the devil's trap" (1 Timothy 3:1–7).

Notice first: "whoever aspires to be an overseer desires a noble task." It is right and good for a man to aspire to eldership in the Church. This is not an ambition born of pride but a holy desire to serve God's people. If the Lord has put this desire in you, do not suppress it. But also do not rush it. Most of the qualifications in this list require years of faithful living to develop.

Notice second: this is a list of character, not a list of gifts. The only gift mentioned is "able to teach." Everything else is about who the man is. He is above reproach — his life has no dirty secret waiting to explode. He is faithful to his wife — "a one-woman man," as the Greek literally says, meaning he is devoted to her alone. He is temperate — not ruled by appetites. He is self-controlled — his mouth, his temper, his desires are governed by the Spirit. He is respectable — his life commands honor without demanding it. He is hospitable — his home is open, his table welcomes guests. He is not given to drunkenness — this is crucial in every culture where alcohol destroys so many homes. He is not violent but gentle. He is not quarrelsome. He is not a lover of money.

Notice third: he must manage his own family well. Paul says if a man cannot shepherd at home, he cannot shepherd in the church. The home is the testing ground. Many men in our churches want the title of elder, the microphone, the respect, the influence — but they have not first proved themselves at home. Their wives fear them. Their children are wild. Their households are in disorder. Such men are not yet ready. Go home, shepherd your wife, raise your children in the Lord, and let the fruit ripen before you grasp for the position.

Notice fourth: he must not be a recent convert. In many rapidly growing churches, this warning is often ignored. We give pulpits to men who have been born again for only a year or two. Sometimes we give them to men who have never been truly converted at all but who have charisma and money. This produces pride in the young leader and disaster in the flock. Let maturity grow. Let character be tested. Let trials be endured. Then lift a man up.

Notice fifth: he must have a good reputation with outsiders. The neighbors who know you — the trader who sells you food, the driver who has carried you, the employee under you — they know if you are a true Christian or only a Sunday one. If the world thinks you are dishonest, a womanizer, a cheat, a bully, you are not qualified to lead the church, no matter how loud you are in worship.

Now, brother, perhaps you are not an elder and never will be. Perhaps you do not aspire to that office. That is fine. Not every man is called to eldership. But every man is called to serve the local church. Hear this clearly: if you are a Christian man, your church needs you, and you need your church.

Think of the church as a body (1 Corinthians 12). Every member contributes something. If the ushers are always the same women, where are the men? If the cleaning of the building falls on the widows, where are the men? If the small group leaders are always the pastor's wife and her friends, where are the men? If the Sunday School teachers are all women, who is modeling Christ for the little boys? If the finances of the church are handled by one tired person, where are the faithful men to bring their wisdom?

Serve where you are needed. Teach if you can teach. Give if you can give. Sing if you can sing.

Fix things if you are handy. Visit the sick. Welcome the newcomer. Pray at prayer meeting. Help with youth events. Disciple a younger man. Support your pastor. Bring a meal to the bereaved family. The body is built up when every part does its work (Ephesians 4:16).

Honor your pastors. Hebrews says, "Have confidence in your leaders and submit to their authority, because they keep watch over you as those who must give an account. Do this so that their work will be a joy, not a burden, for that would be of no benefit to you" (Hebrews 13:17). Your pastor is a man like you, with his own struggles. He needs your prayers, your encouragement, your honest support. Do not gossip about him. Do not undermine him. Do not tear him down behind his back.

If you disagree with him, go to him privately in love.

A word of warning also: do not idolize him. The pastor is a man, not a messiah. Do not build your faith on his personality. In our day, we have seen too many one-man churches where the pastor is treated like a king or a prophet, where no one can question him, where the money flows into his pockets and the building never gets finished. This is not biblical Christianity. Elders — plural — lead the church (Acts 14:23, Titus 1:5). A healthy church has a plurality of qualified men, not a single unaccountable ruler. If your church does not have this, pray for it, work toward it, and perhaps, with humility and patience, help build it.

Consider Athanasius, the great African bishop of Alexandria in the 300s. He is known as "Athanasius against the world" because he stood for the deity of Christ when most of the church had drifted into the Arian heresy. Five times he was exiled by emperors who wanted him to compromise. Five times he returned. He was faithful to the truth of Scripture no matter the cost.

And because one African man would not bow, the Church today still confesses that Jesus is fully God. One faithful elder can change the course of history. Do not think your service is too small to matter.

Consider also the humble pastor in a small village church in some forgotten corner of the world. He will never be famous. He will never write a book. His name will not be remembered in fifty years.

But he prays for his flock. He preaches the Word faithfully Sunday after Sunday. He visits the sick. He buries the dead. He marries the young. He catechizes the children. He will hear one day from Jesus, "Well done, good and faithful servant." That is glory enough. Do not despise such men. Do not leave them alone. Stand with them.

Brother, commit to a local church. Be a member, not a visitor. Be a servant, not just a consumer.

Be present in the joys and the hardships. Be there when the roof leaks and when there is no money for the power bill. Be there when the youth are wild and need godly men. Be there when an elder falls into sin and the church weeps. Be there when revival comes and when seasons are dry. "They devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching and to fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer" (Acts 2:42). So must you.

A Prayer

Father, thank You for Your Church, the body of Christ, the pillar and foundation of the truth. Forgive me for the times I have been a consumer rather than a servant, a critic rather than a builder, a drifter rather than a member. Give me a heart for Your local church. If You are calling me to eldership, prepare me and do not let me run ahead of Your timing. If You are calling me to other service, make me faithful in the smallest task. Help me honor my pastors, support my brothers, and build up the body. Make me a man of whom it may be said, "He loved the Church of God."

In the name of Jesus, the Chief Shepherd, Amen.

fields.title: The Teacher at Home
fields.body_html:
Family Worship and Discipleship

"These commandments that I give you today are to be on your hearts. Impress them on your children. Talk about them when you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up."

— Deuteronomy 6:6–7 The pulpit of the home is greater than the pulpit of the church. This is not because the church pulpit is unimportant — it is vitally important — but because the home pulpit reaches ears that hear you six days a week, not one. Your wife and your children will hear more sermons from you at your dinner table than they will ever hear from the greatest preacher alive. The question is not whether you are teaching them. You are. The question is, what are you teaching them?

If you do not pray with them, you are teaching them prayer is unimportant. If you do not open the Bible with them, you are teaching them the Bible is unimportant. If you do not worship God in the home, you are teaching them worship is for Sunday only. If you never correct them when they dishonor God in speech or action, you are teaching them God's name is not to be feared. You teach, whether you mean to or not. Every father is a pastor of his home, either a faithful one or a negligent one.

Moses told the fathers of Israel to "impress" God's commandments on their children. The Hebrew word is intense — it means to sharpen, to pound in, to engrave. This is not a casual mention. This is intentional, repeated, patient teaching. It is the work of years, not moments.

And when does this teaching happen? "When you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up" (Deuteronomy 6:7). That is, always. In four broad times: at home, on the road, at night, in the morning. This covers a day.

Let me paint a picture for you of what family discipleship can look like. I am not giving a law here, only a shape. Adapt it to your household, your stage of life, your rhythms. But do something.

In the morning, before you scatter to work and school, gather for a short time around the Word.

Read a portion of Scripture — maybe a chapter, maybe just a few verses — and pray together for the day. It does not have to be long. Ten or fifteen minutes is enough. The consistency matters more than the length.

At meals, pray — not the same rote prayer every time, but real thanksgiving. Discuss the day. Ask your children questions about what they are learning. Listen to your wife tell you about her morning. Eat together. Technology down. Screens off. Hearts open.

On the road — meaning in the car, on the walk to school, on the bus, wherever you travel together — talk about God as you go. "Do you see the sunset? What kind of God makes that?"

"Do you remember what the pastor preached about yesterday? What did you think?" "Why do we help that beggar? What does the Bible say?" The road is a classroom for the father.

At night, gather again for family worship. This is the main meal of your spiritual table. Read Scripture, sing a hymn or chorus, pray, perhaps use a catechism to teach the faith. Bless your children one by one before they go to bed. Put your hand on each child's head and pray, "Lord, bless my son. Lord, bless my daughter. Keep them in the faith. Protect them this night. Make them useful to You." Those words will echo in their souls for a lifetime.

Then pray with your wife before you sleep. Confess any sins from the day. Forgive if there has been friction. Intercede for the children, for the family, for the church. End the day as you began it — under the mercy of God. If this sounds overwhelming, take heart. You will not do it perfectly.

You will miss days. Your wife will carry it some days. Your children will roll their eyes at some points. That is fine. You are not trying to create a flawless religious performance. You are trying to weave the gospel into the fabric of your home. The occasional miss is not the issue. The pattern over years is what shapes souls.

Let me recommend a few practical tools. The Psalms are the prayer book of the Bible and a wonderful starting point for family reading. Begin in Psalm 1 and work slowly through. The Gospels — Matthew, Mark, Luke, John — are where your children will meet Jesus; read them repeatedly. Proverbs is full of practical wisdom; read a chapter a day, matching the day of the month. Simple catechisms, like the children's catechism or an age-appropriate confession of faith, can give your family the skeleton of Christian doctrine. Good hymnals or songbooks put theology into song that children remember for life.

Think of Timothy, the young pastor in the New Testament. Paul says to him, "I am reminded of your sincere faith, which first lived in your grandmother Lois and in your mother Eunice and, I am persuaded, now lives in you also" (2 Timothy 1:5). Then later: "But as for you, continue in what you have learned and have become convinced of, because you know those from whom you learned it, and how from infancy you have known the Holy Scriptures" (2 Timothy 3:14–15). From infancy. Lois and Eunice had been teaching Timothy the Scriptures since he was a baby. This is the mother's blessing, but it should also be the father's legacy. What are you teaching your infant?

What is being poured into your toddler? Do not wait until they are teenagers and then expect them to love Jesus. Begin now, with the youngest in the home.

And do not despair if your children are already grown and you feel you missed the window. You did not. You can still repent, apologize to your adult children for past failures, and begin leading them now. Many men, in their fifties and sixties, have been the most powerful spiritual leaders to their adult children — precisely because they humbled themselves and started late with grace. It is better to begin late than never.

Jonathan Edwards, the New England pastor of the 1700s, had eleven children with his wife Sarah.

He prayed for each of them daily. He read the Bible with them. He walked the grounds of his home with them, catechizing, discussing, laughing, teaching. A study of the descendants of Jonathan and Sarah Edwards found over a thousand graduates, pastors, professors, judges, authors, and public servants. That is what happens when a father takes family discipleship seriously. A century later, his great-great-grandchildren were still being shaped by the habits of prayer that began at his hearth.

And do not forget the children of Festo Kivengere and other Ugandan revival fathers. Many of them became pastors, teachers, and faithful servants of the Lord themselves. The fire did not die with the fathers — it was passed. Fathers, wherever you are, pass the fire.

Let me close with a warning and encouragement. The warning: your children will see through hypocrisy. If you teach the Bible at night but live in contradiction by day, they will notice. They will wait until they are old enough to reject the faith, and they will throw it out as something their father only performed. Do not teach what you are not trying to live. Apologize to them when you fail. Show them a father who is being sanctified, not a father who pretends to be already perfect.

The encouragement: God can do more with a sincere, stumbling father than you can imagine. He is the One who works in your children. You plant and water, but He gives the growth (1 Corinthians 3:6–7). Be faithful. Be patient. Be persistent. And trust the God who loves your children more than you do.

A Prayer

Lord God, You are the great Teacher. You taught Israel through Moses, You taught Your disciples as You walked along the road, You teach me still through Your Word and Spirit. Make me a teacher in my own home. Forgive me for the times I have left the spiritual instruction of my family to others. Give me a love for Your Word. Give me patience to teach line by line. Give me wisdom to answer my children's questions. Give me grace to live what I teach. Let our home be a small church where Your Name is loved, Your Word is read, and Your Son is adored. Let my children, when they are old, rise up and call Your name blessed because their father taught them to know You. In Jesus' name, amen.

At night, gather again for family worship. This is the main meal of your spiritual table. Read Scripture, sing a hymn or chorus, pray, perhaps use a catechism to teach the faith. Bless your children one by one before they go to bed. Put your hand on each child's head and pray, "Lord, bless my son. Lord, bless my daughter. Keep them in the faith. Protect them this night. Make them useful to You." Those words will echo in their souls for a lifetime. Then pray with your wife before you sleep. Confess any sins from the day. Forgive if there has been friction. You will miss days. Your wife will carry it some days. Your children will roll their eyes at some points. That is fine. You are not trying to create a flawless religious performance. You are trying to weave the gospel into the fabric of your home. The occasional miss is not the issue. The pattern over years is what shapes souls. Let me recommend a few practical tools. The Psalms are the prayer book of the Bible and a wonderful starting point for family reading. Begin in Psalm 1 and work slowly through. The Gospels — Matthew, Mark, Luke, John — are where your children will meet Jesus; read them repeatedly. Proverbs is full of practical wisdom; read a chapter a day, matching the day of the month. You taught Israel through Moses, You taught Your disciples as You walked along the road, You teach me still through Your Word and Spirit. Make me a teacher in my own home. Give me wisdom to answer my children's questions. Give me grace to live what I teach. Let our home be a small church where Your Name is loved, Your Word is read, and Your Son is adored. fields.title: The Battle Within
fields.body_html:
Fighting Sin and Walking in Purity

"Flee from sexual immorality. All other sins a person commits are outside the body, but whoever sins sexually, sins against their own body."

— 1 Corinthians 6:18 We have spoken much about leadership outside of ourselves — in the home, in the church, in the community. Now we must speak about the hardest leadership of all: the leadership of ourselves.

The war within. The fight for personal holiness.

Brother, you cannot lead others into places where you refuse to go yourself. You cannot call your wife to purity if you are feeding on pornography in secret. You cannot teach your sons self-control if you are mastered by alcohol. You cannot instruct your daughters about modesty if your eyes wander when you walk down the street. The battle within comes before the battle without. Jesus said, "You hypocrite, first take the plank out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother's eye" (Matthew 7:5).

Let us speak honestly about some specific sins that devastate men everywhere.

First, sexual sin. Sexual immorality has been a stumbling block for men since the Garden of Eden, and our generation has no shortage of it. Adultery is everywhere. Pornography is in every pocket that carries a smartphone. Polygamy, though sometimes dressed in cultural clothing, often feeds the same selfish desires. Young men sleep with girlfriends and call it "just how things are."

Older men keep girls on the side and think their wives do not know. Pastors fall. Deacons fall.

Elders fall. The newspapers are full of scandals.

The Bible's command is simple: "Flee from sexual immorality" (1 Corinthians 6:18). Not debate it. Not flirt with it. Not enjoy the edges of it. Flee. Joseph ran from Potiphar's wife so fast he left his cloak behind (Genesis 39:12). That is the pattern. When the temptation comes, your legs are your best friend.

Why flee? Paul gives the answer: your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19).

You are not your own. You were bought at a price. Christ paid for every cell of your body with His blood. To defile what He has bought is to sin not only against your wife, not only against the woman involved, not only against your children, but against Christ Himself.

Practically, how do we flee? Set guardrails. Do not meet alone with a woman who is not your wife, especially not in private settings. Do not text late at night with a woman who is not your wife. Do not keep pornographic material anywhere — on your phone, on your computer, in your mind.

Install accountability software. Confess to a brother when you have stumbled. Do not romanticize your past sins by telling the old stories. Keep your mind and your eyes under the rule of the Spirit.

"I made a covenant with my eyes not to look lustfully at a young woman," said Job (Job 31:1).

Make that same covenant today.

Second, alcohol. This is a plague in many places. Home-brewed spirits, local beers, cheap gin, imported whiskeys — they have destroyed more homes than almost any other single sin. A man goes out after work "just for one drink." He comes home drunk at midnight. His wife smells it. His children see it. His Sunday sermon dies on his lips.

Scripture does not forbid the moderate use of wine (Psalm 104:15, 1 Timothy 5:23). But it repeatedly condemns drunkenness. "Do not get drunk on wine, which leads to debauchery. Instead, be filled with the Spirit" (Ephesians 5:18). "Wine is a mocker and beer a brawler; whoever is led astray by them is not wise" (Proverbs 20:1). "Woe to those who rise early in the morning to run after their drinks, who stay up late at night till they are inflamed with wine" (Isaiah 5:11).

Let me speak clearly. If alcohol has any grip on you at all — if you need it to relax, if you cannot stop at one, if you spend money on it your family needed for food, if you have ever been drunk in front of your children, if your wife has begged you to stop — then you must put it down completely.

Not reduce. Not manage. Stop. The Bible calls it "not given to drunkenness" as a qualification for leadership (1 Timothy 3:3). Many men today cannot lead because they cannot rule their cups.

Third, anger. We have spoken of this in the chapter on gentleness, but it returns here as a deep sin to fight. "In your anger do not sin. Do not let the sun go down while you are still angry, and do not give the devil a foothold" (Ephesians 4:26–27). Uncontrolled anger in a man gives the devil a direct doorway into his home. Many of our fathers passed rage down to us like an inheritance. We can break that chain. We can refuse to pass it to our sons.

Fourth, the love of money and corruption. In many places, bribery is so common it has almost become invisible. Small gifts to get a job done. Larger payments to avoid traffic tickets. Business deals built on kickbacks. Government contracts that line private pockets. Some of this is simply theft from the poor, dressed up in polite language. The Bible is uncompromising: "Whoever loves money never has enough; whoever loves wealth is never satisfied with their income" (Ecclesiastes 5:10). "A greedy man brings ruin to his household" (Proverbs 15:27). "The Lord detests dishonest scales" (Proverbs 11:1).

If you are in a position where you can give or take bribes, there will be a cost to doing it God's way. You may earn less. You may be passed over. You may be laughed at. But "better a little with righteousness than much gain with injustice" (Proverbs 16:8). You cannot serve God and money (Matthew 6:24). Choose today whom you will serve.

Fifth, pride. This is the root of all the others. Pride is the sin that turned an angel into the devil.

Pride says, "I know better than God." Pride says, "The rules do not apply to me." Pride says, "I do not need accountability." Pride says, "I am the head — obey me." Pride is sneaky, and it hides in everything, even our humility. "God opposes the proud but shows favor to the humble" (James 4:6). Brother, take note: God opposes the proud. Not just dislikes. Opposes. Actively works against. Do not let pride sit unchallenged in your heart.

How do we fight these sins? Not by trying harder alone. Willpower fails. Resolutions break. The pattern is always the same: repent, confess, run to Christ, be filled with the Spirit, find a brother to walk with you, stay close to the means of grace.

The Gospel is the engine of your holiness. It is not that Jesus saved you by grace and now you must become holy by sweat. No — "he who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion until the day of Christ Jesus" (Philippians 1:6). The same grace that saved you sanctifies you. You fight sin from a place of acceptance, not for acceptance. Your Father already loves you. Your failures do not drive Him away. They drive you to Him.

Consider Augustine of Hippo once more. He struggled with sexual sin for years. He famously prayed, "Lord, grant me chastity — but not yet!" He knew what was right, but he could not walk in it. When he finally broke through, it was not by his own strength. He was weeping in a garden, heard a child's voice saying "take and read," opened the Bible, and read Romans 13:13–14: "Let us behave decently, as in the daytime, not in carousing and drunkenness, not in sexual immorality and debauchery, not in dissension and jealousy. Rather, clothe yourselves with the Lord Jesus Christ." The light flooded in. The chains snapped. The power of the gospel broke through.

Your breakthrough will come the same way. Not by grit, but by grace. Not by hiding, but by bringing your sin into the light. Not by self-righteousness, but by the righteousness of Christ laid hold of by faith. "It is for freedom that Christ has set us free. Stand firm, then, and do not let yourselves be burdened again by a yoke of slavery" (Galatians 5:1).

So fight, brother. Fight every day. Fight with your Bible open. Fight with your knees bent. Fight with brothers beside you. Fight with your wife aware. Fight with the Holy Spirit as your strength.

And know this: in Jesus Christ, you are on the winning side.

A Prayer

Holy God, You are light, and in You there is no darkness at all. I confess I have walked in dark places. I have loved sins that You hate. I have fed desires that will destroy me. Have mercy on me, a sinner. Wash me whiter than snow. Break the power of every sin that has bound me — every lust, every bottle, every outburst, every bribe, every secret pride. Crucify my flesh with its passions and desires. Fill me with Your Holy Spirit. Give me brothers to fight beside me. Make me a man who walks in the light, who confesses quickly, who runs to Christ when he falls. And in the end, present me faultless before the presence of Your glory with great joy. In the name of Jesus, who is mighty to save, amen.

fields.title: Vision and Stewardship
fields.body_html:
Setting Godly Goals

"Then the Lord replied: 'Write down the revelation and make it plain on tablets so that a herald may run with it.'"

— Habakkuk 2:2 A man without vision is a drifter. He may work hard, but he does not know where he is going. He may make money, but he does not know what for. He may raise children, but he does not know what he wants to pass to them. Life happens to him, rather than him living life on purpose.

Solomon wrote, "Where there is no vision, the people perish" (Proverbs 29:18, in the older translation). The newer translations put it, "Where there is no revelation, people cast off restraint."

Both ideas are true. A man who has not heard from God about his life, and who has not put his vision on paper, lives without direction and often without restraint.

God is a God of plans. "For I know the plans I have for you," declares the Lord, "plans to prosper you and not to harm you, plans to give you hope and a future" (Jeremiah 29:11). If God plans for your life, should you not also plan with Him? Many Christian men mistake "waiting on the Lord" for passivity. They do nothing and call it faith. But biblical waiting is active. Nehemiah prayed for four months before he acted (Nehemiah 1–2), but when he acted, he had a plan. He counted the days, surveyed the walls, organized the workers, assigned the gates.

Brother, have you set godly goals for your life? Not the world's kind of goals — a bigger car, a bigger house, a bigger title — but goals shaped by Scripture and aimed at the glory of God?

Goals for your walk with Christ? Goals for your marriage? Goals for your children? Goals for your work? Goals for your giving? Goals for your local church? Goals for your nation?

Let me help you think in categories.

Spiritual goals. Where do you want to be with Christ in one year, five years, twenty years? Do you have a plan to read through the Bible? Do you have a plan to memorize Scripture? Do you have a plan for prayer? Do you have books you intend to read to grow in theology and pastoral wisdom?

Ask God to show you the man He wants you to become spiritually, and then ask Him how to get there.

Marriage goals. What kind of husband do you want to be in ten years? What does your wife most need from you this year — healing from some past wound? More time? More prayer? Better communication? Sit down with her and ask. Then write it down. Without a goal for your marriage, you will drift into mediocrity.

Family goals. What do you want to pass to your children? Not just money — character, faith, skills, a love of learning, a love of the Church, a heart for the lost. Name what you want them to know, what you want them to believe, what you want them to be. Then design your fatherhood toward those goals.

Work goals. What is God calling you to do with your hands and your mind? If you are an employee, how will you become excellent? If you are a business owner, what ethical and profitable path lies ahead? If you are a farmer, what is the plan for this season's planting and for five years from now?

Do not drift in your work. Plan it.

Financial goals. What is your plan for saving, giving, investing, and providing? Proverbs says, "The plans of the diligent lead to profit as surely as haste leads to poverty" (Proverbs 21:5). Have a household budget. Set aside for your children's school fees. Give to your local church regularly.

Save for emergencies. Plan for old age. Avoid ruinous debt. These are not optional for a godly man.

Service goals. How do you want to serve God's people? What gifts has He given you, and how will you use them? Maybe you want to disciple three young men next year. Maybe you want to help plant a church. Maybe you want to start a ministry for widows in your community. Dream with God. Write it down.

Habakkuk was told to "write down the revelation and make it plain on tablets, so that a herald may run with it" (Habakkuk 2:2). Write your vision. Get it on paper, or on your phone, or in a notebook.

There is something holy about writing. It forces you to think clearly. It makes the vision survive when your memory fails. It lets you review and adjust. Begin today. Just a page. A few lines under each category. You can refine it over time.

Then pray over your vision regularly. Lay it before the Lord. Say, "Father, if this is not from You, kill it. If this is from You, bring it to pass. I submit every goal to Your will." "Commit to the Lord whatever you do, and he will establish your plans" (Proverbs 16:3). Remember also, "Many are the plans in a person's heart, but it is the Lord's purpose that prevails" (Proverbs 19:21). Your goals are not God's orders to Him. They are your honest desires submitted to His sovereign hand.

Stewardship is the twin of vision. If God has given you a life, you are to steward it. If He has given you money, time, talents, children, a wife, influence — all these are on loan. "Now it is required that those who have been given a trust must prove faithful" (1 Corinthians 4:2). The parable of the talents (Matthew 25:14–30) is clear: the Master will return and ask what you did with what He gave you. The man who buried his talent in fear was called wicked and lazy. The men who invested and multiplied were welcomed into the joy of their Master.

Do not bury your talents, brother. Do not sit on your hands because you feel small. Do not say, "I am only a farmer, a driver, a clerk, a young man." God gave you your talents. Use them. Start where you are. Trade faithfully. Grow what He has given.

A simple tool: every Sunday evening, look at the week ahead. What are your priorities? Your Bible reading plan? One concrete way you will serve your wife this week? One thing you will teach your children? One person you will disciple or encourage? One hour you will give to the local church?

One person you will pray for by name? Plan it. Then do it. A year of such weeks changes a life.

Consider William Wilberforce, the English Christian statesman of the late 1700s. He set himself "two great objects": the abolition of the slave trade and the reformation of manners (moral renewal of society). He wrote these goals down. He pursued them for decades. He did not live to see all the fruit, but he changed the British Empire. One man with a clear, God-given vision can move mountains.

Consider also African brothers who have done the same. Samuel Ajayi Crowther, a Nigerian who was rescued from a slave ship as a boy, set himself to translate the Bible into his mother tongue and to plant the Church among his people. He did it. Today the Yoruba church is one of the strongest in Africa partly because a man set a godly goal and worked toward it for the rest of his life.

Dream big dreams for God, but be faithful in small daily steps. "Do not despise these small beginnings, for the Lord rejoices to see the work begin" (Zechariah 4:10). The oak tree is in the acorn. The revival is in the prayer meeting of three men. The great marriage is in the daily kindness of a husband. The godly son is in the bedtime prayer of a father. Plant well and the harvest will come.

A Prayer

Father, You are the God who plans from eternity past to eternity future, the God who numbered my days before one of them came to be. Give me Your vision for my life. Break me free from drifting. Break me free from mediocrity. Break me free from burying my talents in fear. Show me what You are calling me to do, to become, and to leave behind. Give me the discipline to write down what You reveal. Give me the wisdom to plan carefully. Give me the faith to trust You with the outcome.

Let my life not be wasted. Use every year, every week, every hour for Your glory.

And at the end of my days, may I hear from You, "Well done." In Jesus' name, Amen.

Let me help you think in categories. Spiritual goals. Where do you want to be with Christ in one year, five years, twenty years? Do you have a plan to read through the Bible? Do you have a plan to memorize Scripture? Do you have a plan for prayer? Do you have books you intend to read to grow in theology and pastoral wisdom? Ask God to show you the man He wants you to become spiritually, and then ask Him how to get there. Marriage goals. What kind of husband do you want to be in ten years? What does your wife most need from you this year — healing from some past wound? More time? More prayer? Better communication? Sit down with her and ask. Then write it down. Without a goal for your marriage, you will drift into mediocrity. Family goals. What do you want to pass to your children? Not just money — character, faith, skills, a love of learning, a love of the Church, a heart for the lost. Name what you want them to know, what you want them to believe, what you want them to be. Then design your fatherhood toward those goals. Work goals. What is God calling you to do with your hands and your mind? If you are an employee, how will you become excellent? If you are a business owner, what ethical and profitable path lies ahead? If you are a farmer, what is the plan for this season's planting and for five years from now? Do not drift in your work. Plan it. Financial goals. What is your plan for saving, giving, investing, and providing? Proverbs says, "The plans of the diligent lead to profit as surely as haste leads to poverty" (Proverbs 21:5). Have a household budget. Set aside for your children's school fees. Give to your local church regularly. Save for emergencies. Plan for old age. Avoid ruinous debt. These are not optional for a godly man. Service goals. How do you want to serve God's people? What gifts has He given you, and how will you use them? Maybe you want to disciple three young men next year. Maybe you want to help plant a church. Maybe you want to start a ministry for widows in your community. Dream with God. Write it down. Habakkuk was told to "write down the revelation and make it plain on tablets, so that a herald may run with it" (Habakkuk 2:2). Write your vision. Get it on paper, or on your phone, or in a notebook. There is something holy about writing. It forces you to think clearly. It makes the vision survive when your memory fails. It lets you review and adjust. Begin today. Just a page. A few lines under each category. You can refine it over time. Then pray over your vision regularly. Lay it before the Lord. Say, "Father, if this is not from You, kill it. If this is from You, bring it to pass. I submit every goal to Your will." "Commit to the Lord whatever you do, and he will establish your plans" (Proverbs 16:3). Remember also, "Many are the plans in a person's heart, but it is the Lord's purpose that prevails" (Proverbs 19:21). Your goals are not God's orders to Him. They are your honest desires submitted to His sovereign hand. Stewardship is the twin of vision. If God has given you a life, you are to steward it. If He has given you money, time, talents, children, a wife, influence — all these are on loan. "Now it is required that those who have been given a trust must prove faithful" (1 Corinthians 4:2). The parable of the talents (Matthew 25:14–30) is clear: the Master will return and ask what you did with what He gave you. The man who buried his talent in fear was called wicked and lazy. The men who invested and multiplied were welcomed into the joy of their Master. Do not bury your talents, brother. Do not sit on your hands because you feel small. Do not say, "I am only a farmer, a driver, a clerk, a young man." God gave you your talents. Use them. Start where you are. Trade faithfully. Grow what He has given. A simple tool: every Sunday evening, look at the week ahead. What are your priorities? Your Bible reading plan? One concrete way you will serve your wife this week? One thing you will teach your children? One person you will disciple or encourage? One hour you will give to the local church? One person you will pray for by name? Plan it. Then do it. A year of such weeks changes a life. Consider William Wilberforce, the English Christian statesman of the late 1700s. He set himself "two great objects": the abolition of the slave trade and the reformation of manners (moral renewal of society). He wrote these goals down. He pursued them for decades. He did not live to see all the fruit, but he changed the British Empire. One man with a clear, God-given vision can move mountains. Consider also African brothers who have done the same. Samuel Ajayi Crowther, a Nigerian who was rescued from a slave ship as a boy, set himself to translate the Bible into his mother tongue and to plant the Church among his people. He did it. Today the Yoruba church is one of the strongest in Africa partly because a man set a godly goal and worked toward it for the rest of his life. Dream big dreams for God, but be faithful in small daily steps. "Do not despise these small beginnings, for the Lord rejoices to see the work begin" (Zechariah 4:10). The oak tree is in the acorn. The revival is in the prayer meeting of three men. The great marriage is in the daily kindness of a husband. The godly son is in the bedtime prayer of a father. Plant well and the harvest will come. A Prayer Father, You are the God who plans from eternity past to eternity future, the God who numbered my days before one of them came to be. Give me Your vision for my life. Break me free from drifting. Break me free from mediocrity. Break me free from burying my talents in fear. Show me what You are calling me to do, to become, and to leave behind. Give me the discipline to write down what You reveal. Give me the wisdom to plan carefully. Give me the faith to trust You with the outcome. Let my life not be wasted. Use every year, every week, every hour for Your glory. And at the end of my days, may I hear from You, "Well done." In Jesus' name, Amen.

fields.title: A Legacy That Outlives You
fields.body_html:
Leaving a Godly Heritage

"A good person leaves an inheritance for their children's children, but a sinner's wealth is stored up for the righteous."

— Proverbs 13:22 You will die, brother. I do not say this to be dark. I say it because the Bible says it. "It is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment" (Hebrews 9:27). Your days are numbered (Psalm 90:12). The length of your life is a secret kept by the One who gave it to you. Some men get eighty years. Some men do not see their fortieth birthday. Some men are cut down at twenty-five, leaving a young wife and small children. None of us know.

But this much we do know: you will leave something behind. Every man does. The question is not whether you will leave a legacy. The question is what kind.

Solomon tells us, "A good person leaves an inheritance for their children's children." Notice the horizon. Not just for your children, but for your children's children — the grandchildren you may or may not live to see. A godly man thinks generationally. He is not building only for his lifetime.

He is building for generations he will not meet on this side of eternity.

What kind of legacy should a godly man aim for? Let us consider three levels: material, moral, and spiritual.

First, a material inheritance. Scripture does honor the passing of material goods. "Houses and wealth are inherited from parents," says Proverbs 19:14.

A father who leaves his family with nothing when he could have planned better has not served them well. This does not mean you must become rich. It means you must be faithful. If you have a small plot of land, can you leave it free of debt? If you have a small business, can you leave it in good health? If you have little to leave, can you leave a legacy of honest dealing with those you owed? Some men leave debts and lawsuits behind them — that is a curse to their children. Some leave paid-up accounts and quiet consciences — that is a blessing.

Plan for what happens when you die. Write a will. In many cultures, when the husband dies without a will, the extended family may come and take what was meant for the widow and the children. Protect your household. A will is not lack of faith; it is an act of love. "The prudent see danger and take refuge, but the simple keep going and pay the penalty" (Proverbs 27:12).

Second, a moral inheritance. This is more valuable than money, and many poor men have left enormous moral wealth to their descendants.

A moral inheritance is the memory of integrity. It is your children saying, "Papa never lied to us."

It is your neighbors saying, "Your father never cheated me." It is your wife saying, "Your father never once raised his hand against me." A reputation for honesty is a shelter that covers your children's children.

A moral inheritance is also the memory of love. It is your grown son remembering, "Papa took me fishing. Papa prayed for me at my bedside. Papa told me he was proud of me." It is your grown daughter remembering, "Papa treated Mama with respect. Papa hugged me. Papa told me I was beautiful in the Lord." Children who are loved well by their fathers are anchored for life.

A moral inheritance is the shape of how you lived. Your working hard. Your faithfulness to one wife. Your kindness to the poor. Your refusal to take bribes. Your laughter in your home. Your songs on the road. Your tears at the funeral of a friend. Your courage at the funeral of a child.

These memories are currency your children will spend for the rest of their lives.

Third, and most important, a spiritual legacy. This is the treasure that outlives every other. "Houses and wealth are inherited from parents, but a prudent wife is from the Lord" (Proverbs 19:14) — how much more is a prudent faith? Money is eaten by inflation and sometimes by corrupt officials.

Land can be stolen. Buildings can burn. Reputations can fade. But a grandchild who knows Jesus because his grandfather prayed for him — that is a legacy no fire can touch, no thief can steal, no government can confiscate.

Think again of Timothy, who had the faith that "first lived in your grandmother Lois and in your mother Eunice" (2 Timothy 1:5). Three generations of faith. A grandmother who loved Jesus, a mother who loved Jesus, a grandson who became a pastor and apostolic helper because of them.

This is a family we do not hear much about by name, but their legacy shaped the Church forever through Timothy's ministry.

Think of the Wesley family. Susanna Wesley, mother of John and Charles, raised nineteen children in a small English parsonage. She taught them the Scriptures. She prayed for them daily. Two of them — John and Charles — shook the world through the Methodist revival, which reached across England, America, and yes, eventually the continent of Africa. Susanna could not have known that her patient mothering would one day result in churches planted in Uganda. But that is how legacy works. A mother's prayers in 1710 became a missionary's boat sailing in 1870 became an African pastor's sermon in 2026.

Think of the East African Revival fathers — Nsibambi, Nagenda, Kivengere, and many more whose names are not as famous but whose prayers and lives touched generations. Kivengere lived to see his preaching impact churches on three continents. His legacy is not a monument of stone; it is souls in glory, churches still preaching the gospel, children of converts still walking with Jesus.

And think of the Ugandan martyrs. Young men, most of them teenagers and young adults, burned alive at Namugongo in 1886. They did not leave behind material wealth. Many had no children.

But look what they left behind: a Church. A century and a half later, more than 80% of Uganda professes the name of Christ because of the witness of those young men. Their blood became seed, just as Tertullian said centuries earlier, "The blood of the martyrs is the seed of the Church." Every June 3rd, Catholics and Protestants alike still remember them. The smallest spiritual legacy is larger than the grandest earthly one.

So what will your legacy be?

Brother, begin now to live with your end in mind. Every day, ask, "If I died tonight, what would my wife remember? What would my children inherit? What would my church say at my funeral?

What would the Lord Jesus say when He meets me?" This is not morbid. This is wisdom. "Teach us to number our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom" (Psalm 90:12).

Live in such a way that when you are old, you can sit and look at your grandchildren and know that you planted well. Live in such a way that when you die, your children say, "Our father loved Jesus, and he loved us." Live in such a way that long after the last person who remembers your face has also died, your great-great-grandchildren are still walking with the Lord because of the family you planted for Him.

The trees you plant today will give shade to generations who will never know your name. Plant well.

A Prayer

Eternal Father, the generations come and go, but You remain forever. My days are a breath; Your years have no end. Teach me to live with eternity in view. Let me not waste my one short life on trivial things. Let me lay down a spiritual heritage that will echo through my family long after my bones rest in the earth. Give me grace to love my wife so well that my granddaughters will expect to be loved well.

Give me grace to teach my children so faithfully that my great-grandchildren will sing Your praises. Let the trees I plant give shade to many. And may my name be found written in the Book of Life when the final day comes. In the name of Jesus Christ, the Resurrection and the Life, Amen.

CONCLUSION Rise Up, Men of God A Call to Action and Closing Prayer

We have come to the end of this journey, brother, but your journey is only beginning.

We began by looking at the hungry land around us — hungry for godly men. We looked at God's creation design, at the inner man, at the power of prayer, at the husband's calling to love, at the father's duty to disciple, at the gentleness of true strength, at the dignity of work, at the watchman's duty of protection, at the iron of accountability, at service in the local church, at the pulpit of the home, at the war within against sin, at the vision of a well-planned life, and at the legacy that reaches far beyond our own grave.

Fourteen chapters. Fourteen calls. Fourteen areas where God has spoken. And now the book closes, and the question presses: what will you do?

Reading is easy. Applying is hard. Books can be set on a shelf and forgotten, or they can be the match that lights a fire. Which will this book be for you?

Let me lay before you a simple call to action. Not complicated. Not overwhelming. Just a beginning. Take what follows and make it your own, with your pastor, with your wife, with your brothers in the faith.

First, make sure you are a Christian. I ask this of every reader, because no one can lead spiritually who has not first been made alive by the Spirit of God. Have you come to the end of yourself and found only Jesus is enough? Have you repented of your sins and trusted in Christ alone for salvation? If you have never done this, do it today. Right where you are. "If you declare with your mouth, 'Jesus is Lord,' and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved" (Romans 10:9). Do not read another chapter of your life without settling this.

Second, commit to a few specific changes. Not all fourteen at once — you cannot carry all of it at the same moment. But pick two or three areas where the Lord has most convicted you, and begin there. Perhaps it is morning prayer. Perhaps it is speaking gently to your wife. Perhaps it is putting away alcohol. Perhaps it is starting family worship. Perhaps it is joining a men's accountability group. Pick two or three and commit before God, in writing if possible, with a witness if possible, to begin.

Third, go to your wife and tell her. Do not promise what you cannot deliver. Simply say, "I have been reading about what God expects of me as a husband and father. I see that I have failed in some areas. I am asking God to change me, and I am asking you to pray for me." Most wives, on hearing such words from their husbands, will weep tears of joy and will pray down heaven upon you. A humble husband is a powerful husband.

Fourth, go to your children, one at a time, and speak to them. If you have harmed them, confess it.

If you have been absent, tell them you are coming home. If you have never blessed them, lay your hand on their head tonight and bless them by name. "The Lord bless you and keep you; the Lord make his face shine on you and be gracious to you; the Lord turn his face toward you and give you peace" (Numbers 6:24–26). That old blessing, spoken over your children tonight, may echo in them for eighty years.

Fifth, find a brother. Do not walk alone. Today, tomorrow at the latest, reach out to one godly man in your church and ask him to meet with you regularly. Tell him, "I am trying to become the man God is calling me to be. Will you walk with me? Will you pray with me? Will you ask me hard questions?" You may be surprised how many men have been waiting for someone to ask them.

Sixth, plant yourself deeply in a local church. Not just attendance — membership, service, submission to elders, participation in the body. Be there in the joys and the struggles. If your current church is not preaching the gospel faithfully and teaching the Word carefully, pray about this with your wife and seek a church that does. But do not be a drifter. The Church is the bride of Christ. Love what He loves.

Seventh, write your vision. Following Habakkuk's instruction, sit down this week — even for thirty minutes — and write what God is calling you to in each area of life. Spiritual. Marriage. Children.

Work. Finance. Service. Let it be imperfect. Refine it over time. But get something on paper. Pray over it. Act on it.

Eighth, pick up this book again in one year. Read it again. See where God has changed you. See where you still need to grow. Let it be a marker on your journey. Share it with another man who needs to read it.

And now, my brother, hear the final word.

Your family, your church, your community — your nation, wherever God has placed you — is waiting for men like you, men who will rise from their knees with the name of Jesus on their lips and the courage of the Spirit in their hearts.

The great fathers of the East African church — Charles Lwanga at Namugongo, Simeon Nsibambi on Namirembe Hill, Festo Kivengere in exile, Janani Luwum before the dictator — they fought the good fight.

They finished the race. They kept the faith (2 Timothy 4:7). They have passed the torch.

Now it is your hand that holds it.

Will you take up the torch, or will you let it fall?

The devil hates a rising man. He will oppose you. He will tempt you. He will try to use your own past failures to convince you it is hopeless. Do not listen. "Greater is he who is in you than he who is in the world" (1 John 4:4). The same Christ who conquered death conquers your fear. The same Spirit who raised Jesus from the dead will raise you from your spiritual sleep.

Rise up, husband. Your wife has been praying for this day.

Rise up, father. Your children have been waiting for you to lead.

Rise up, brother. The church of God needs your shoulder beside theirs.

Rise up, man of God. The nations are watching. Heaven is watching. The Lord Jesus Christ is watching. And one day you will stand before Him and give an account.

May you stand on that day, not trembling in shame, but joyful, weary but not ashamed, your hands rough from faithful labor, your family standing behind you, your brothers beside you, your Savior's words ringing in your ears: "Well done, good and faithful servant. Enter into the joy of your Lord."

Amen, and Amen.

Closing Prayer

Our Father in heaven, hallowed be Your name. Your kingdom come, Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. Lord Jesus Christ, You who walked the earth as the perfect Man, the true Husband of the Church, the great Son of the Father, we lift our eyes to You now. Holy Spirit, without whom nothing true can be done, we ask You to fall fresh upon us. We come before You, Father, as men. Some of us are young, some old. Some married, some still waiting. Some have fathered children well, some have failed them deeply. Some have walked with You for years, some are only just beginning. But all of us, in this moment, bow before You and say: we are Yours. Forgive us for the years we have lived for ourselves. Forgive us for the wives we have not loved as Christ loved the Church. Forgive us for the children we have not discipled, the homes we have not led, the churches we have not served, the sins we have not confessed, the brothers we have not supported. Wash us in the blood of Jesus. Clothe us in His righteousness. Fill us with His Spirit. And send us out as men. Make us men who pray before they speak. Men who confess before they accuse. Men who love before they demand. Men who serve before they command.

Men who work hard and trust You for the harvest. Men who stand as watchmen at the gates of our homes. Men who plant ourselves in Your Church and do not drift away. Men who fight the battle within and walk in the purity Your Son bought with His blood. Men of vision. Men of faithfulness. Men who leave behind a legacy that will sing Your praises for generations. For our wives, O Lord, have mercy. For our children, make us the fathers You have called us to be. For our churches, raise us up as servants and elders. For our nations — wherever we live, on every continent — send us a revival like the East African Revival, the fire that fell in the 1930s, a fire that humbles men, purifies families, strengthens churches, and shakes whole nations. We long to see it. We pray for it.

We will be ready for it. Bless the wives who are reading this prayer beside their husbands, those who have prayed for years and are about to see the answer. Bless the single men who are preparing for a holy marriage one day. Bless the widowers who feel alone. Bless the young men who have no father in the home, and be their Father Yourself. Bless the elders of the Church who are weary in shepherding.

Bless the pastors who plead in empty sanctuaries. Bless the evangelists who still walk the village paths with Bibles in hand. And when our days are done, Lord, let us stand before You with joy. Let none of our family be missing at the Wedding Supper of the Lamb. Let our labor not be in vain. Let our lives sing of Your goodness long after our graves have grown quiet. We ask all this in the mighty, glorious, saving, sanctifying name of the Lord Jesus Christ, our Savior, our Lord, our Brother, our King. Amen.

THE END

If you have never blessed them, lay your hand on their head tonight and bless them by name. "The Lord bless you and keep you; the Lord make his face shine on you and be gracious to you; the Lord turn his face toward you and give you peace" (Numbers 6:24–26). That old blessing, spoken over your children tonight, may echo in them for eighty years. Fifth, find a brother. Do not walk alone. Today, tomorrow at the latest, reach out to one godly man in your church and ask him to meet with you regularly. Tell him, "I am trying to become the man God is calling me to be. Will you walk with me? Will you pray with me? Will you ask me hard questions?" You may be surprised how many men have been waiting for someone to ask them. Sixth, plant yourself deeply in a local church. Not just attendance — membership, service, submission to elders, participation in the body. Be there in the joys and the struggles. If your current church is not preaching the gospel faithfully and teaching the Word carefully, pray about this with your wife and seek a church that does. But do not be a drifter. The Church is the bride of Christ. Love what He loves. Seventh, write your vision. Following Habakkuk's instruction, sit down this week — even for thirty minutes — and write what God is calling you to in each area of life. Spiritual. Marriage. Children. Work. Finance. Service. Let it be imperfect. Refine it over time. But get something on paper. Pray over it. Act on it. Eighth, pick up this book again in one year. Read it again. See where God has changed you. See where you still need to grow. Let it be a marker on your journey. Share it with another man who needs to read it. And now, my brother, hear the final word. Your family, your church, your community — your nation, wherever God has placed you — is waiting for men like you, men who will rise from their knees with the name of Jesus on their lips and the courage of the Spirit in their hearts. The great fathers of the East African church — Charles Lwanga at Namugongo, Simeon Nsibambi on Namirembe Hill, Festo Kivengere in exile, Janani Luwum before the dictator — they fought the good fight. They finished the race. They kept the faith (2 Timothy 4:7). They have passed the torch. Now it is your hand that holds it. Will you take up the torch, or will you let it fall? The devil hates a rising man. He will oppose you. He will tempt you. He will try to use your own past failures to convince you it is hopeless. Do not listen. "Greater is he who is in you than he who is in the world" (1 John 4:4). The same Christ who conquered death conquers your fear. The same Spirit who raised Jesus from the dead will raise you from your spiritual sleep. Rise up, husband. Your wife has been praying for this day. Rise up, father. Your children have been waiting for you to lead. Rise up, brother. The church of God needs your shoulder beside theirs. Rise up, man of God. The nations are watching. Heaven is watching. The Lord Jesus Christ is watching. And one day you will stand before Him and give an account. May you stand on that day, not trembling in shame, but joyful, weary but not ashamed, your hands rough from faithful labor, your family standing behind you, your brothers beside you, your Savior's words ringing in your ears: "Well done, good and faithful servant. Enter into the joy of your Lord." Amen, and Amen. Closing Prayer Our Father in heaven, hallowed be Your name. Your kingdom come, Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. Lord Jesus Christ, You who walked the earth as the perfect Man, the true Husband of the Church, the great Son of the Father, we lift our eyes to You now. Holy Spirit, without whom nothing true can be done, we ask You to fall fresh upon us. We come before You, Father, as men. Some of us are young, some old. Some married, some still waiting. Some have fathered children well, some have failed them deeply. Some have walked with You for years, some are only just beginning. But all of us, in this moment, bow before You and say: we are Yours. Forgive us for the years we have lived for ourselves. Forgive us for the wives we have not loved as Christ loved the Church. Forgive us for the children we have not discipled, the homes we have not led, the churches we have not served, the sins we have not confessed, the brothers we have not supported. Wash us in the blood of Jesus. Clothe us in His righteousness. Fill us with His Spirit. And send us out as men. Make us men who pray before they speak. Men who confess before they accuse. Men who love before they demand. Men who serve before they command. Men who work hard and trust You for the harvest. Men who stand as watchmen at the gates of our homes. Men who plant ourselves in Your Church and do not drift away. Men who fight the battle within and walk in the purity Your Son bought with His blood. Men of vision. Men of faithfulness. Men who leave behind a legacy that will sing Your praises for generations. For our wives, O Lord, have mercy. For our children, make us the fathers You have called us to be. For our churches, raise us up as servants and elders. For our nations — wherever we live, on every continent — send us a revival like the East African Revival, the fire that fell in the 1930s, a fire that humbles men, purifies families, strengthens churches, and shakes whole nations. We long to see it. We pray for it. We will be ready for it. Bless the wives who are reading this prayer beside their husbands, those who have prayed for years and are about to see the answer. Bless the single men who are preparing for a holy marriage one day. Bless the widowers who feel alone. Bless the young men who have no father in the home, and be their Father Yourself. Bless the elders of the Church who are weary in shepherding. Bless the pastors who plead in empty sanctuaries. Bless the evangelists who still walk the village paths with Bibles in hand. And when our days are done, Lord, let us stand before You with joy. Let none of our family be missing at the Wedding Supper of the Lamb. Let our labor not be in vain. Let our lives sing of Your goodness long after our graves have grown quiet. We ask all this in the mighty, glorious, saving, sanctifying name of the Lord Jesus Christ, our Savior, our Lord, our Brother, our King. Amen. THE END
